items.q: Can a Court take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 67 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, if the wife does not file a complaint against the husband, when the persons involved are in a marital relationship?
items.ref: No, it cannot.

A1.t:
**Answer.** A Court can take cognizance of an offence under section 67 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, even if the wife does not file a complaint against the husband, provided the persons involved are in a marital relationship.

**Why.** Section 67 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, specifically allows for the prosecution of certain offences without a complaint being filed by the victim, including where the victim is a spouse.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §67

A2.t:
**Answer.** No, a Court cannot take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 67 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, if the wife does not file a complaint against the husband, when the persons involved are in a marital relationship.

**Why.** The statute specifically provides that a Court shall not take cognizance of such an offence unless the wife files a complaint against the husband, and the Court is satisfied that the facts constituting the offence are prima facie.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §221

A3.t:
**Answer.** No, the Court cannot take cognizance of such an offence unless the wife files a complaint.

**Why.** The law mandates that for offences defined in section 67, the Court must be satisfied that the wife has filed a complaint before it can take cognizance. This requirement applies specifically to offences committed by a husband against his wife.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §219

A4.t:
**Answer.** No, the Court cannot take cognizance of such an offence unless the wife files a complaint against the husband, and the Court is satisfied that the facts constitute the offence.

**Why.** The law mandates that no Court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 67 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, where the persons are in a marital relationship, unless the wife files a complaint against the husband. This requirement applies even if the Court determines that the facts constitute the offence.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §221

items.q: Can a complainant withdraw their complaint against multiple accused, and if so, what is the effect?
items.ref: Yes, a complainant can withdraw their complaint against all or any of the accused, and the Magistrate shall acquit the accused accordingly.

A1.t:
**Answer.** A complainant can withdraw their complaint against one or more accused at any time before the conclusion of the trial.

**Why.** The complainant has the right to withdraw the complaint without prejudice to their ability to file a fresh complaint later if they wish to pursue the matter further.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** Yes, a complainant can withdraw their complaint against one or more of the accused before a final order is passed.

**Why.** This allows the complainant to terminate the prosecution against certain accused if they no longer wish to pursue charges, provided there are sufficient grounds for doing so. This ensures that the process remains fair and responsive to the interests of justice.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §280

A3.t:
**Answer.** Yes, a complainant may withdraw his complaint against any of the accused persons.

**Why.** The law allows a complainant to withdraw his complaint against any of the accused persons. This withdrawal can be done at any time before the trial begins.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §245

A4.t:
**Answer.** Yes, a complainant can withdraw their complaint against multiple accused, and this withdrawal results in an acquittal for those accused against whom the complaint is withdrawn.

**Why.** The law allows a complainant to withdraw their complaint against multiple accused before a final order is passed. This withdrawal leads to an acquittal for the accused against whom the complaint is withdrawn, provided the conviction is not set aside.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §280

items.q: Can a creditor's release of one co-surety free the released surety from responsibility to the other sureties?
items.ref: No, the released surety remains responsible to the other sureties.

A1.t:
**Answer.** A creditor's release of one co-surety does not free the released surety from responsibility to the other sureties.

**Why.** Each surety in a joint liability agreement remains individually responsible to the extent of their obligation until the debt is fully discharged. Therefore, the release of one surety does not discharge the entire debt, leaving the remaining sureties still liable.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** Yes, a creditor's release of one co-surety does not discharge the others; neither does it free the released surety from his responsibility to the other sureties.

**Why.** This rule ensures that the responsibility among co-sureties remains intact unless all co-sureties are released by the creditor. It prevents any single co-surety from being unfairly relieved of their obligations.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §138

A3.t:
**Answer.** No, the release of one co-surety does not discharge the released surety from his liability to the remaining sureties.

**Why.** The law stipulates that the release of one co-surety does not discharge the released surety from his liability to the remaining sureties. This liability remains intact even after the release.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §145

A4.t:
**Answer.** No, the release of one co-surety does not free the released surety from responsibility to the other sureties.

**Why.** The law dictates that where there are co-sureties, a release by the creditor of one of them does not discharge the others. This means the released surety remains responsible to the remaining sureties.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §138

items.q: Can a person who furnishes necessaries to an incapable person's family members be reimbursed from the incapable person's property?
items.ref: Yes, if the necessaries supplied are suitable to the condition in life of the incapable person's family members, the person who furnished the necessaries is entitled to be reimbursed from the incapable person's property.

A1.t:
**Answer.** A person who has furnished necessaries to an incapable person's family members can be reimbursed from the incapable person's property.

**Why.** The law allows reimbursement from the property of an incapable person for necessaries supplied to their family members, ensuring that essential needs are met even if the incapable person cannot provide for them.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §56

A2.t:
**Answer.** Yes, a person who furnishes necessaries to an incapable person's family members can be reimbursed from the incapable person's property.

**Why.** The statute explicitly states that if a person supplies necessaries to someone who is legally bound to support, the supplier is entitled to reimbursement from the incapable person's property. This applies to both the incapable person and their family members who are legally bound to be supported.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §68

A3.t:
**Answer.** Yes, the person may be reimbursed from the property of the incapable person.

**Why.** The law provides that if a person has furnished necessaries to the family of an incapable person, they have a right to be reimbursed from the property of that person.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §378

A4.t:
**Answer.** Yes, the person who has supplied the necessaries is entitled to be reimbursed from the property of the incapable person.

**Why.** The law provides that if a person supplies necessaries to someone who is either incapable of contracting or legally bound to support, the supplier is entitled to reimbursement from the property of that person. This entitlement applies even when the person receiving the necessities is a family member.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §68

items.q: Can an assembly become unlawful after it has assembled?
items.ref: Yes, an assembly that was not unlawful when it assembled may subsequently become an unlawful assembly.

A1.t:
**Answer.** An assembly becomes unlawful only if it was lawful to begin with but subsequently violates the provisions of the law.

**Why.** Once an assembly has legally convened, it can only be rendered unlawful through subsequent actions that contravene the law, such as engaging in activities forbidden during the assembly.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** Yes, an assembly which was not unlawful when it assembled, may subsequently become an unlawful assembly.

**Why.** The law recognizes that an assembly's status as unlawful can change over time based on the actions and intentions of its members. Once it becomes clear that the assembly has a common object that falls under the definition of an unlawful assembly, it transforms into one regardless of its initial legality.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §189

A3.t:
**Answer.** Yes, an assembly can become unlawful even after it has assembled.

**Why.** The law provides that an assembly is unlawful if it is convened or held for the purpose of committing an offence, regardless of whether the assembly has already assembled.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §149

A4.t:
**Answer.** Yes, an assembly that was not unlawful when it assembled may subsequently become an unlawful assembly.

**Why.** The law provides that an assembly which was not unlawful when it assembled may subsequently become an unlawful assembly. This change in status can occur if the common object of the persons composing the assembly falls into one of the categories listed in sub-section (1).

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §189

items.q: Can an offender be punished more severely for an offence that is a combination of separate acts that would each be punishable by a different punishment?
items.ref: The offender shall not be punished with a more severe punishment than the Court which tries him could award for any one of such offences.

A1.t:
**Answer.** An offender can be punished according to the most severe punishment applicable to any of the separate acts, but not exceeding the maximum punishment for the most serious act.

**Why.** This rule ensures that the punishment reflects the seriousness of the most egregious act while adhering to the principle of proportionality. It prevents the cumulative effect of multiple punishments from being excessively harsh.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §105

A2.t:
**Answer.** No, the offender cannot be punished more severely than the maximum punishment for any single offence among the combined acts.

**Why.** The law limits the cumulative punishment to the highest penalty applicable to any single offence among the combined acts to prevent excessive sentencing.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §9

A3.t:
**Answer.** No, the offender cannot be punished with a punishment that is more severe than the punishment provided for any one of the acts.

**Why.** The law stipulates that if an offence is committed by doing two or more things, and each act would be punishable by a distinct punishment, the offender shall not be punished with a punishment that is more severe than the punishment provided for any one of those acts.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §145

A4.t:
**Answer.** No, the offender shall not be punished with a more severe punishment than the Court which tries him could award for any one of such offences.

**Why.** The law dictates that where several acts combine to form a different offence, the offender cannot be punished with a more severe penalty than the Court could award for any single offence. This limitation applies even if the acts individually would warrant different punishments.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §9

items.q: Can the principal be held responsible for the acts of the person employed as a sub-agent without the agent's authority?
items.ref: No, the principal is not responsible for the sub-agent's acts.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The principal cannot be held responsible for the acts of the person employed as a sub-agent without the agent's authority.

**Why.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, specifically provides that an agent who exceeds his authority does so at his own risk and the principal is not bound by such unauthorized acts.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §149

A2.t:
**Answer.** No, the principal is not represented by or responsible for the acts of the person so employed.

**Why.** The law clearly states that where an agent appoints a person without authority, the agent stands in the relation of a principal to an agent and is responsible for the acts of the person appointed, while the principal is neither represented nor responsible for those acts.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §193

A3.t:
**Answer.** I don't have enough information in the source material to answer that.

**Why.** Answering this would require the specific rules governing the liability of the principal when the agent acts beyond their authority, which the source material does not address.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §205

A4.t:
**Answer.** No, the principal is not represented by or responsible for the acts of the person so employed, nor is that person responsible to the principal.

**Why.** The law establishes that when an agent appoints a person without authority, the agent assumes the role of a principal to an agent. This means the agent is responsible to the principal and to third parties, but the principal remains unrepresented by the actions of this sub-agent.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §193

items.q: How are words used in describing an offence to be understood in a charge?
items.ref: They will be deemed to have the sense attached to them by the law under which the offence is punishable.

A1.t:
**Answer.** Words used in describing an offence shall be understood according to their common meaning unless a different meaning is provided by the statute.

**Why.** This rule ensures clarity and consistency in interpreting offences, preventing any ambiguity that could lead to misinterpretation or misuse of the law. It adheres to the principle of giving effect to the ordinary meaning of words used in statutes.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §5

A2.t:
**Answer.** Words used in describing an offence in a charge shall be deemed to have been used in the sense attached to them respectively by the law under which such offence is punishable.

**Why.** This ensures clarity and consistency in interpreting the terms used to describe an offence, thereby providing the accused with a clear understanding of the charges against them.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §237

A3.t:
**Answer.** Words used in describing an offence must be construed as including the corresponding words of the opposite gender.

**Why.** The law mandates that when words are used in describing an offence, they shall be construed as including the corresponding words of the opposite gender.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §219

A4.t:
**Answer.** Words used in describing an offence shall be deemed to have been used in the sense attached to them respectively by the law under which such offence is punishable.

**Why.** The law mandates that when an offence is charged, the words used to describe that offence must be interpreted according to the specific meaning assigned to them by the law defining that offence.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §237

items.q: In a contract where one party's promise cannot be claimed until the other party's promise has been performed, what is the consequence if the second party fails to perform their promise?
items.ref: The first party cannot claim the performance of the second party's promise and must make compensation for any loss sustained.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The first party is discharged from their obligation under the contract.

**Why.** When one party's obligation is contingent upon the performance of another party's obligation, failure by the latter to perform discharges the former from their duty under the contract.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §26

A2.t:
**Answer.** The first party cannot claim the performance of the reciprocal promise and must make compensation to the other party for any loss sustained due to the non-performance of the contract.

**Why.** This rule ensures fairness in contractual obligations by allowing the party who has fulfilled their part of the agreement to seek compensation when the other party fails to meet their obligations, thus preventing one party from being unjustly enriched at the expense of the other.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §54

A3.t:
**Answer.** The first party is not entitled to claim payment of the promised consideration.

**Why.** If the performance of one party's promise is dependent on the performance of another party's promise, and that second party fails to perform, the first party loses the right to claim payment for their own promise.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §50

A4.t:
**Answer.** The first party cannot claim the performance of the reciprocal promise, and they must make compensation to the other party for any loss sustained due to the non-performance of the contract.

**Why.** If a contract involves reciprocal promises, and the second party fails to perform their promise, the first party loses the right to claim performance of the reciprocal promise. Furthermore, the first party is required to compensate the other party for any loss suffered due to the non-performance of the contract.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §54

items.q: In what circumstance does a surgeon, who makes a communication to a patient for the patient's benefit, avoid committing an offence?
items.ref: If the communication is made in good faith and the patient dies as a consequence of the communication, but not as a result of the surgeon's intention.

A1.t:
**Answer.** A surgeon avoids committing an offence when making a communication to a patient for the patient's benefit if the communication is made in good faith and in the course of his profession.

**Why.** The statute provides that certain communications made by professionals, including surgeons, for the benefit of their patients are exempted from being considered as offences under the medical practice laws, provided they are made in good faith and within the scope of their professional duties.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §45

A2.t:
**Answer.** A surgeon avoids committing an offence when making a communication to a patient for the patient's benefit, provided the communication is made in good faith and does not cause harm to the patient.

**Why.** The law specifically protects communications made in good faith for the benefit of the patient, even if such communications result in harm to the patient. This ensures that healthcare professionals can provide necessary information without fear of legal repercussions, as long as their intentions are benevolent.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §31

A3.t:
**Answer.** The surgeon is not liable if the communication is made in good faith and for the benefit of the patient.

**Why.** A surgeon is exempt from liability if the communication is made in good faith and for the benefit of the patient. This exemption applies regardless of whether the communication is made before or after the operation.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §294

A4.t:
**Answer.** The surgeon avoids committing an offence if the communication is made in good faith and for the benefit of the patient, regardless of whether the patient dies as a result of the communication.

**Why.** The law provides that no communication made in good faith is an offence by reason of any harm to the person to whom it is made, provided the communication is made for the benefit of that person. This protection applies even if the patient dies as a result of the communication.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §31

items.q: In what circumstances can a court direct that an offender's imprisonment be wholly or partly rigorous?
items.ref: In cases where an offender is punishable with imprisonment which may be of either description.

A1.t:
**Answer.** A court may direct that an offender's imprisonment be wholly or partly rigorous if the offence is punishable with rigorous imprisonment.

**Why.** The court has discretion to order rigorous imprisonment when the nature of the offence warrants it, ensuring that the punishment fits the crime more precisely.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §95

A2.t:
**Answer.** A court can direct that an offender's imprisonment be wholly or partly rigorous in any case where the offender is punishable with imprisonment which may be of either description.

**Why.** The law provides that in such cases, the court has the discretion to specify whether the imprisonment should be wholly rigorous, wholly simple, or a combination of both, depending on the nature of the offense and the sentence imposed.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §7

A3.t:
**Answer.** A court may order rigorous imprisonment if the offender is sentenced to imprisonment for life, or if they are sentenced to imprisonment for a term exceeding two years.

**Why.** The power to order rigorous imprisonment applies when the sentence is for life or for a term exceeding two years. This power is exercised by the court when it passes the sentence.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §451

A4.t:
**Answer.** A court may direct that the entire period of imprisonment be rigorous, or that any part of the period be rigorous, when sentencing an offender who is liable to both simple and rigorous imprisonment.

**Why.** The law provides that in every case where an offender is liable to both simple and rigorous imprisonment, the court has the power to direct the nature of the imprisonment. This direction can specify whether the entire period should be rigorous, or whether a specific part of the period should be rigorous.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §7

items.q: In what circumstances can a person's action, which may appear to be an offence, be justified?
items.ref: When a person believes himself to be justified by law, in good faith, and not by reason of a mistake of law.

A1.t:
**Answer.** A person's action that may appear to be an offence can be justified if it is done to prevent a greater evil or to protect a greater right.

**Why.** The law recognizes the principle of necessity, allowing actions that might otherwise be considered offences if they are taken to avert a more serious harm or to protect a significant right of another individual.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** A person's action may be justified if it is done by law, or if the person believes in good faith that it is justified by law, or if it is done accidentally without any criminal intention or knowledge.

**Why.** The law provides several scenarios where actions that might otherwise be considered offences can be justified. These include situations where the action is legally mandated, where the person reasonably believes the action is necessary under the law, or where the action occurs by accident without any criminal intent.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §17

A3.t:
**Answer.** An act that would otherwise be an offence is not an offence if it is done in good faith for the benefit of the person who does it.

**Why.** The law provides an exception where an act that would otherwise constitute an offence is performed in good faith and for the benefit of the person performing it. This exception applies regardless of whether the act is done for the benefit of another person or for the benefit of the person themselves.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §15

A4.t:
**Answer.** An action is not an offence if it is done by a person who is justified by law, or who by reason of a mistake of fact and not by reason of a mistake of law in good faith, believes himself to be justified by law in doing it.

**Why.** The law provides that nothing is an offence if it is done by a person who is justified by law, or who by reason of a mistake of fact and not by reason of a mistake of law in good faith, believes himself to be justified by law in doing it. This justification applies to actions taken in good faith while exercising powers granted by law.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §17

items.q: In what circumstances may the Judge permit evidence of one alleged fact to be given before another alleged fact is proved?
items.ref: The relevancy of one alleged fact depends upon another alleged fact being first proved.

A1.t:
**Answer.** A judge may permit evidence of one alleged fact to be given before another alleged fact is proved if it is necessary to make the proof of the first fact effective.

**Why.** This provision allows for the admissibility of evidence in a manner that ensures the integrity and coherence of the trial process, ensuring that relevant evidence can be presented in a logical sequence when it is necessary for the understanding and evaluation of the facts.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** The Judge may permit evidence of one alleged fact to be given before another alleged fact is proved if the relevancy of the first fact depends on the second fact being first proved, and this decision is within the Judge’s discretion.

**Why.** This rule allows flexibility in the presentation of evidence to ensure that the relevance of each fact is appropriately considered. The Judge can decide whether to admit evidence in a sequence that best supports the case, balancing the need for relevant evidence with the logical flow of the argument.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §141

A3.t:
**Answer.** The Judge may permit this if they consider that the evidence of the first fact is relevant to the second fact.

**Why.** The Judge has the discretion to permit evidence of one fact to be given before another fact is proved. This permission is granted only when the Judge determines that the evidence of the first fact is relevant to the second fact.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §154

A4.t:
**Answer.** The Judge may permit evidence of one fact to be given before another fact is proved if the relevancy of the first fact depends on the second fact being proved, or if the Court determines that the first fact should be proven before the second fact.

**Why.** The Judge has the discretion to either permit the evidence of the first fact to be given before the second fact is proved, or to require the evidence of the second fact to be given before the evidence of the first fact is permitted. This decision is based on the dependency of the relevancy of the first fact on the second fact.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §141

items.q: In what manner must the information about persons arrested, charges, and offences be prominently displayed in every police station and at the district headquarters?
items.ref: In any manner including in digital mode.

A1.t:
**Answer.** Information regarding persons arrested, the charges against them, and the offences committed must be displayed in a conspicuous manner.

**Why.** This ensures transparency and accountability, allowing the public to access information about ongoing cases and the status of individuals held in custody. The display must be in a way that it can be easily seen by anyone visiting the police station or district headquarters.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** The information about persons arrested, charges, and offences must be prominently displayed in any manner, including in digital mode, in every police station and at the district headquarters.

**Why.** This ensures transparency and public access to information regarding arrests, thereby promoting accountability and public trust in the police force.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §37

A3.t:
**Answer.** The information must be displayed in a conspicuous place within the police station and at the district headquarters.

**Why.** The law mandates that the information regarding persons arrested, the charges against them, and the offences committed must be displayed in a conspicuous place within the police station and also at the district headquarters.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §59

A4.t:
**Answer.** The information must be displayed in a manner that includes digital mode.

**Why.** The law mandates that the State Government must establish a police control room in every district and at the State level. Furthermore, the information concerning the names and addresses of persons arrested, the nature of the offence, and the charge must be displayed in every police station and at the district headquarters. This display must occur in a manner that includes digital mode.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §37

items.q: In what type of examination may leading questions be asked without limitation?
items.ref: In cross-examination, leading questions may be asked without limitation.

A1.t:
**Answer.** Leading questions may be asked without limitation in cross-examination.

**Why.** The rule allows for thorough testing of the witness's statements during cross-examination, ensuring that the truth is revealed.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §65

A2.t:
**Answer.** Leading questions may be asked in cross-examination without limitation.

**Why.** The statute specifically permits leading questions during cross-examination, indicating no restrictions apply in this context.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §146

A3.t:
**Answer.** Leading questions may be asked in an examination-in-chief.

**Why.** Leading questions are permitted during the examination-in-chief. This exception applies only to the examination-in-chief and not to any other stage of the trial.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §316

A4.t:
**Answer.** Leading questions may be asked during cross-examination.

**Why.** The law permits leading questions to be asked during cross-examination, regardless of whether the adverse party objects to them. This exception applies even if the Court has not granted specific permission.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §146

items.q: In what types of proceedings is the husband or wife of the accused a competent witness?
items.ref: Criminal proceedings.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The husband or wife of the accused is not a competent witness in any proceedings against the accused.

**Why.** This rule is designed to prevent bias and ensure fair trials by excluding potential witnesses who may be influenced by their relationship to the accused.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** In criminal proceedings against any person, the husband or wife of such person is a competent witness for the defence.

**Why.** The law specifically allows the spouse of the accused to testify in criminal cases, provided the spouse requests to do so in writing. This rule ensures that spouses can provide necessary evidence without being compelled to do so.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §353

A3.t:
**Answer.** The husband or wife of the accused is a competent witness in any inquiry, trial, or other proceeding under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.

**Why.** The law specifies that the husband or wife of the accused is a competent witness in any inquiry, trial, or other proceeding under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §316

A4.t:
**Answer.** The husband or wife of the accused is a competent witness in both civil and criminal proceedings.

**Why.** The law establishes that the husband or wife of any party to a suit is a competent witness in civil proceedings. Furthermore, the husband or wife of the accused is a competent witness in criminal proceedings against the accused.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §126

items.q: In which situations may the cross-examination of a witness be deferred?
items.ref: The Judge may, in his discretion, permit the cross-examination of any witness to be deferred until any other witness or witnesses have been examined or recall any witness for further cross-examination.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The cross-examination of a witness may be deferred if the court considers it necessary for the proper disposal of the case.

**Why.** The court has discretion to defer cross-examination to ensure that all relevant evidence is properly examined and that justice is done. This can include cases where additional time is needed to prepare for the examination or when the interests of justice so require.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §154

A2.t:
**Answer.** The cross-examination of a witness may be deferred until any other witness or witnesses have been examined or for further cross-examination.

**Why.** This flexibility allows the court to manage the order of examination and cross-examination effectively, ensuring that all relevant aspects of the case are thoroughly explored while maintaining the efficiency of the proceedings.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §254

A3.t:
**Answer.** The cross-examination may be deferred if the Court determines that it is necessary for the proper disposal of the case.

**Why.** The cross-examination of a witness can be deferred if the Court considers it necessary for the proper disposal of the case. This deferral must be made with the consent of the parties.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §319

A4.t:
**Answer.** Cross-examination may be deferred if the Judge determines it is necessary, or if the Judge recalls a witness for further cross-examination.

**Why.** The law provides that the cross-examination of a witness may be deferred by the Judge's discretion. This deferral can occur either when the Judge deems it necessary, or when the Judge recalls a witness specifically for further cross-examination.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §254

items.q: Is the rescinding party required to perform any promises they made in the contract?
items.ref: No, the rescinding party is not required to perform any promises they made in the contract.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The rescinding party is not required to perform any promises they made under the contract once it has been rescinded.

**Why.** When a contract is rescinded, it is as if the contract never existed. Therefore, the obligations and promises made under the contract are nullified, and the parties are restored to their original positions.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §24(2)

A2.t:
**Answer.** The rescinding party need not perform any promise therein contained in which they are promisor.

**Why.** When a contract is rescinded, the party who rescinds is relieved of their obligations under the contract, including the promises they made. However, they must return any benefits received from the other party under the contract.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §64

A3.t:
**Answer.** The rescinding party is not required to perform any promise that was made by them under the contract.

**Why.** The law provides that when a contract is rescinded, the rescinding party is exempt from performing any promise that was made by them under the contract.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §56

A4.t:
**Answer.** No, the party who rescinds the contract is not required to perform any promise contained within the contract where they are the promisor.

**Why.** When a person at whose option a contract is voidable rescinds it, the other party is not required to perform any promise contained in the contract where that person is the promisor. Furthermore, the party who rescinds the contract must restore any benefit received from the other party, if possible.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §64

items.q: To whom is the agent responsible for the acts of the sub-agent appointed without authority?
items.ref: The agent is responsible for the sub-agent's acts both to the principal and to third persons.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The principal is responsible for the acts of the sub-agent appointed without authority.

**Why.** When an agent appoints a sub-agent without authority, the principal remains liable for the unauthorized acts of the sub-agent, unless the principal can prove that they took reasonable steps to prevent such appointment or were unaware of it.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §145

A2.t:
**Answer.** The agent stands towards such a person in the relation of a principal to an agent and is responsible for his acts both to the principal and to third persons.

**Why.** When an agent appoints a sub-agent without having the necessary authority to do so, the agent assumes the role of a principal towards the sub-agent and becomes responsible for the actions of the sub-agent. This means the agent must account for any actions taken by the sub-agent to both the principal and any third parties involved.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §193

A3.t:
**Answer.** The agent is responsible to the principal for all acts done by the sub-agent.

**Why.** When an agent appoints a sub-agent without authority, the agent remains responsible to the principal for all acts performed by that sub-agent.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §204

A4.t:
**Answer.** The agent is responsible to the principal for the acts of the sub-agent.

**Why.** When an agent appoints a person without authority, the agent assumes the role of a principal to an agent. This means the agent is responsible to the principal for the acts committed by the sub-agent.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §193

items.q: To whom must a person aware of the commission of, or intention to commit, an offence punishable under the specified sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, forthwith give information?
items.ref: The nearest Magistrate or police officer.

A1.t:
**Answer.** A person aware of the commission of, or intention to commit, an offence punishable under the specified sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita must forthwith give information to the nearest police station.

**Why.** Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, it is the duty of every citizen to report any criminal activity or the intent to commit a crime to the authorities to ensure public safety and uphold the law.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §25

A2.t:
**Answer.** Every person aware of the commission of, or intention to commit, an offence punishable under the specified sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, must forthwith give information to the nearest Magistrate or police officer.

**Why.** This provision aims to ensure that individuals who are aware of criminal activities report them immediately to the authorities to prevent further harm and facilitate prompt action by law enforcement.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §33

A3.t:
**Answer.** The information must be given to any police officer or any other person in charge of a police station.

**Why.** A person who knows that an offence has been committed or is about to be committed must immediately inform either a police officer or the person in charge of a police station.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §194

A4.t:
**Answer.** The person must give information to the nearest Magistrate or police officer.

**Why.** The law mandates that every person who is aware of the commission of, or the intention of another person to commit, any of the specified offences must immediately provide information to the nearest Magistrate or police officer.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §33

items.q: To whom or what must the police officer or other person making the arrest deliver any offensive weapons taken from the person arrested?
items.ref: The police officer or other person making the arrest must deliver all weapons taken to the Court or officer.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The police officer or other person making the arrest must deliver any offensive weapons taken from the person arrested to the nearest police station.

**Why.** This ensures that seized items are properly accounted for and can be examined to confirm their nature and to determine if further action is necessary.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §45

A2.t:
**Answer.** The police officer or other person making the arrest must deliver any offensive weapons taken from the person arrested to the Court or officer before whom the officer or person making the arrest is required to produce the person arrested.

**Why.** This ensures that the weapons taken during the arrest are accounted for and can be inspected by the judicial authority overseeing the case, thereby maintaining transparency and accountability in the handling of arrested individuals and their belongings.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §50

A3.t:
**Answer.** The person must deliver the weapons to the person who made the arrest.

**Why.** The law mandates that the person who makes the arrest must be the recipient of the weapons. This delivery is required when the person arrested is released on their own bond or bail bond.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §51

A4.t:
**Answer.** The police officer or other person making the arrest must deliver all offensive weapons taken from the person arrested to the Court or officer before whom the officer or person making the arrest is required to produce the person arrested.

**Why.** The law mandates that the police officer or other person making the arrest must deliver all offensive weapons taken from the person arrested to the Court or officer before whom the officer or person making the arrest is required to produce the person arrested.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §50

items.q: Under what circumstances can a Court publish a written proclamation requiring a person to appear at a specified place and time?
items.ref: The Court has reason to believe that the person against whom a warrant has been issued has absconded or is concealing himself, making it impossible to execute the warrant.

A1.t:
**Answer.** A Court can publish a written proclamation requiring a person to appear at a specified place and time when the person has absconded after being summoned to appear.

**Why.** This provision allows the court to ensure compliance with its summons, especially when the accused has deliberately avoided appearing before the court, thereby facilitating the administration of justice.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §154

A2.t:
**Answer.** A Court can publish a written proclamation if it believes that a person against whom a warrant has been issued has absconded or is concealing himself, making the warrant unexecutable.

**Why.** This provision allows the Court to take additional steps to ensure the appearance of a person who has evaded a warrant, thereby facilitating the execution of legal processes and ensuring justice is served.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §84

A3.t:
**Answer.** A Court may issue such a proclamation if it has reason to believe that the person is likely to commit an offence or to be absent from the Court when required.

**Why.** The power to issue a written proclamation is triggered when a Court believes that a person is likely to commit an offence or is likely to be absent from the Court when they are required to attend.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §145

A4.t:
**Answer.** A Court may publish a written proclamation if it believes, after taking evidence, that a person against whom a warrant has been issued has absconded or is concealing himself so that the warrant cannot be executed.

**Why.** The power to publish a written proclamation arises when a Court determines, after taking evidence, that a person against whom a warrant has been issued has absconded or is concealing himself. This action is taken because the warrant cannot be executed.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §84

items.q: Under what circumstances can a Court take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 67 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, when the persons involved are in a marital relationship?
items.ref: Only when the wife files a complaint against the husband, after prima facie satisfaction of the facts that constitute the offence.

A1.t:
**Answer.** A Court can take cognizance of an offence under section 67 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, even if the persons involved are in a marital relationship, provided the offence is reported by a third party or a public servant.

**Why.** The law allows for exceptions to the general rule that a husband cannot be prosecuted for an offence committed against his wife without her consent, to ensure that victims of domestic violence or abuse can seek justice.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §67(3)

A2.t:
**Answer.** A Court can take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 67 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, when the persons involved are in a marital relationship, if a complaint has been filed or made by the wife against the husband.

**Why.** The statute specifically provides that cognizance can only be taken upon a complaint filed by the wife against the husband in a marital relationship, unless there is prima facie satisfaction of the facts constituting the offence.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §221

A3.t:
**Answer.** The Court may take cognizance if it is satisfied that there is reasonable ground to believe that the offence has been committed and that the person accused is likely to be found within its local jurisdiction.

**Why.** The Court must first be satisfied that there is a reasonable ground to believe that the offence has been committed and that the person accused is likely to be found within the local jurisdiction. This requirement applies specifically when the offence is committed by a person against whom a decree for maintenance has been passed.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §218

A4.t:
**Answer.** A Court cannot take cognizance of such an offence unless it is satisfied that the facts constituting the offence have been established through a complaint filed by the wife against the husband.

**Why.** The law mandates that no Court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 67 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, if the persons are in a marital relationship, unless the Court is satisfied that the facts constituting the offence have been established through a complaint filed by the wife against the husband.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §221

items.q: Under what circumstances can a Magistrate direct the sale of perishable property?
items.ref: If the person entitled to the possession of such property is unknown or absent and the property is subject to speedy and natural decay, or if the Magistrate to whom its seizure is reported is of opinion that its sale would be for the benefit of the owner, or that the value of such property is less than ten thousand rupees.

A1.t:
**Answer.** A Magistrate can direct the sale of perishable property if it is necessary to prevent waste or damage to the property.

**Why.** The Magistrate has the discretion to take such action to ensure that perishable goods are not wasted or damaged while in their custody.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §154

A2.t:
**Answer.** A Magistrate can direct the sale of perishable property if it is ordered to be attached and if the Court thinks it expedient.

**Why.** This provision allows for the immediate sale of perishable goods to prevent loss or deterioration, ensuring that the property is managed in a way that preserves its value and utility.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §85

A3.t:
**Answer.** A Magistrate may direct the sale if they believe that the property is likely to perish or deteriorate before it can be sold.

**Why.** The power to direct sale is triggered when the Magistrate determines that the property is likely to perish or deteriorate before it can be sold. This determination must be made in the absence of any person who has an interest in the property.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §495

A4.t:
**Answer.** A Magistrate may direct the sale of perishable property if the person entitled to possession is unknown or absent, or if the Magistrate believes the sale would benefit the owner or if the property's value is less than ten thousand rupees.

**Why.** The power to sell perishable property arises when the person entitled to possession is unknown or absent, or when the Magistrate determines that the sale would be beneficial to the owner or that the property's value is less than ten thousand rupees.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §505

items.q: Under what circumstances can a Magistrate take cognizance of an offence on his own knowledge?
items.ref: When he has information that such offence has been committed

A1.t:
**Answer.** A Magistrate can take cognizance of an offence on his own knowledge if the offence is bailable, triable by summary trial, and not compoundable except by law.

**Why.** This provision allows a Magistrate to initiate proceedings without a complaint from a victim or a police report under certain conditions to ensure that minor offences are promptly addressed. The restriction to bailable, triable by summary trial, and non-compoundable offences ensures that serious crimes are not improperly handled by a Magistrate.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §154

A2.t:
**Answer.** A Magistrate can take cognizance of an offence on his own knowledge if he receives information from any person other than a police officer or based on his own knowledge that such an offence has been committed.

**Why.** This provision allows for the initiation of legal proceedings based on direct observation or reliable reports from individuals outside the formal reporting mechanisms, ensuring that potential crimes are not overlooked.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §210(c)

A3.t:
**Answer.** A Magistrate may take cognizance of any offence that he has reason to believe has been committed, provided the offence is not one for which the law requires previous sanction.

**Why.** The power to take cognizance on own knowledge applies when a Magistrate believes an offence has been committed. This power exists only if the offence is not one that requires previous sanction from the Central Government or the State Government.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §219

A4.t:
**Answer.** A Magistrate can take cognizance of an offence based on information received from any person other than a police officer, or based on his own knowledge that the offence has been committed.

**Why.** A Magistrate may take cognizance of an offence if the information comes from any person other than a police officer, or if the Magistrate has knowledge that the offence has been committed. This provision allows the Magistrate to initiate the process based on these sources of information.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §210

items.q: Under what circumstances can a complainant withdraw their complaint against an accused?
items.ref: The complainant can withdraw their complaint if there are sufficient grounds for permitting them to do so, as determined by the Magistrate.

A1.t:
**Answer.** A complainant can withdraw a complaint against an accused at any time before the trial begins.

**Why.** The right to withdraw a complaint is a fundamental right of the complainant, ensuring that they can discontinue proceedings if they so choose without facing undue legal or procedural barriers.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** A complainant can withdraw their complaint against an accused at any time before a final order is passed, provided they satisfy the Magistrate that there are sufficient grounds for doing so. Alternatively, the Magistrate may permit withdrawal on their own accord if there are multiple accused and the complainant consents to withdrawing the charge against some but not all of them.

**Why.** This provision allows flexibility in the criminal justice process, enabling the complainant to reconsider their decision to pursue charges against the accused. It ensures that the Magistrate can intervene if necessary to prevent frivolous or vexatious complaints.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §280

A3.t:
**Answer.** A complainant may withdraw the complaint at any time before the case is finally disposed of.

**Why.** The law allows a complainant to withdraw the complaint at any time before the case has been finally disposed of. This withdrawal must be made in writing and must be filed with the Court.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §245

A4.t:
**Answer.** A complainant may withdraw their complaint if they satisfy the Magistrate that there are sufficient grounds for doing so, either before a final order is passed or before the charge is framed.

**Why.** The law allows a complainant to withdraw their complaint if they satisfy the Magistrate that there are sufficient grounds for doing so. This withdrawal must occur either before a final order is passed in any case under this Chapter or before the charge is framed.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §280

items.q: Under what circumstances can a confession made by a person in police custody be proved against them?
items.ref: No confession made by any person while he is in the custody of a police officer, unless it is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate shall be proved against him.

A1.t:
**Answer.** A confession made by a person in police custody can be proved against them only if it was voluntarily made and not obtained through coercion, threat, or promise of reward.

**Why.** According to the law, confessions obtained under duress are considered unreliable and inadmissible to prevent the misuse of power by authorities. This rule ensures that only voluntary confessions are used in court to uphold the integrity of the judicial process.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** A confession made by a person in police custody can only be proved against them if it is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate, except when the information leading to the discovery of a fact was received from a person in police custody.

**Why.** The law aims to protect the rights of individuals by limiting the admissibility of confessions made under duress or without proper oversight. Confessions made in the presence of a Magistrate ensure that the confession is voluntary and not coerced.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §23

A3.t:
**Answer.** A confession is admissible if it is made by the accused while in police custody and is recorded in writing under the hand of an officer not below the rank of sub-inspector.

**Why.** The law allows for the admission of a confession made by the accused while in police custody. This confession must be recorded in writing and must be signed by an officer who holds a rank no lower than that of a sub-inspector.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §164

A4.t:
**Answer.** A confession made by a person in police custody cannot be proved against them unless it is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate, or if the confession is made to a police officer who has been given powers by a Magistrate under any law for the time being in force.

**Why.** The law prohibits the use of any confession made by a person in police custody as evidence against them, unless the confession is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate. This restriction applies even if the confession is made to a police officer who has been given powers by a Magistrate under any law for the time being in force.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §23

items.q: Under what circumstances can an Executive Magistrate require a person to show cause why they should not be ordered to execute a bond or bail bond?
items.ref: The circumstances are when a person is taking precautions to conceal their presence and there is reason to believe they are doing so with a view to committing a cognizable offence.

A1.t:
**Answer.** An Executive Magistrate can require a person to show cause when there are reasonable grounds to believe that the person has committed an offense under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023.

**Why.** This provision ensures that before imposing a bond or bail, the Executive Magistrate must first hear the individual's explanation regarding the alleged offense to ensure that the order is justified and fair.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** An Executive Magistrate can require a person to show cause why they should not be ordered to execute a bond or bail bond if the Magistrate receives information that the person is taking precautions to conceal their presence with a view to committing a cognizable offence, or if the person is likely to commit a breach of the peace or disturb the public tranquillity.

**Why.** The law allows an Executive Magistrate to take preventive measures by requiring a bond or bail bond from a person suspected of future criminal activity, either to prevent the commission of a cognizable offence or to maintain public order and tranquillity.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §128

A3.t:
**Answer.** An Executive Magistrate may require a person to show cause if the person is required to execute a bond or bail bond for their own appearance before the Magistrate.

**Why.** The power to require a person to show cause is triggered when the person is required to execute a bond or bail bond for their own appearance before the Magistrate. This requirement must be made in writing and must be served on the person.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §125

A4.t:
**Answer.** An Executive Magistrate can require a person to show cause if the Magistrate receives information that the person is taking precautions to conceal their presence and that there is reason to believe they are doing so with a view to committing a cognizable offence.

**Why.** The power to require a person to show cause arises when an Executive Magistrate receives information that a person is taking precautions to conceal their presence and that there is reason to believe they are doing so with a view to committing a cognizable offence. This requirement must be made in the manner provided by the law.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §128

items.q: Under what circumstances can the Court dispense with the translation of evidence taken down in English?
items.ref: When under clause (b) evidence is taken down in English and a translation thereof in the language of the Court is not required by any of the parties, the Court may dispense with such translation.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The Court may dispense with the translation of evidence taken down in English if it finds that the language of the evidence is understood by the parties and the witnesses.

**Why.** This provision aims to ensure efficiency and fairness in the proceedings by allowing the use of the language that all parties comprehend, thereby avoiding unnecessary delays caused by translation.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** When the evidence is taken down in English and a translation into the language of the Court is not required by any of the parties, the Court may dispense with such translation.

**Why.** The statute allows for the dispensation of translation when it is not necessary according to the parties involved, ensuring efficiency and reducing unnecessary administrative burden while respecting the rights of the parties to understand the proceedings.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §312

A3.t:
**Answer.** The Court may dispense with the translation if it is satisfied that the evidence has been taken down in a language other than English and that the language used is one that is generally understood by the parties to the suit.

**Why.** The Court has the power to dispense with the translation of evidence if it determines that the evidence was taken down in a language other than English. This dispensation applies specifically when the language used is one that is generally understood by the parties to the suit.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §319

A4.t:
**Answer.** The Court may dispense with the translation of evidence taken down in English if the evidence is not required by any of the parties.

**Why.** The law provides that when evidence is taken down in English, a translation into the language of the Court must be prepared. However, this requirement is subject to a specific exception: the Court may dispense with the translation if the evidence is not required by any of the parties.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §312

items.q: Under what circumstances can the bail required by a police officer or Magistrate be reduced?
items.ref: The High Court or the Court of Session may direct that the bail be reduced.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The bail can be reduced if the Magistrate is satisfied that the ends of justice would be served thereby.

**Why.** The law allows for the reduction of bail to ensure that the administration of justice is not obstructed and that the interests of justice are met. This provision ensures that the bail amount is not unnecessarily high, thus facilitating the release of the accused while ensuring that the trial proceeds smoothly.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §154

A2.t:
**Answer.** The bail required by a police officer or Magistrate can be reduced by the High Court or the Court of Session.

**Why.** The authority to reduce bail lies with higher judicial bodies to ensure that the bail set is appropriate and not excessive given the circumstances of the case.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §484

A3.t:
**Answer.** The bail may be reduced if the person is willing to give security for their appearance before the Magistrate.

**Why.** If a person is willing to give security for their appearance before the Magistrate, the bail amount may be reduced. This reduction applies when the person is required to appear before the Magistrate.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §78

A4.t:
**Answer.** The High Court or the Court of Session may direct that the bail required by a police officer or Magistrate be reduced.

**Why.** The power to reduce bail is vested in the High Court or the Court of Session. This power allows them to direct that the bail required by a police officer or Magistrate be reduced.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §484

items.q: Under what circumstances can the conclusive proof of legitimacy be overturned?
items.ref: The conclusive proof can be overturned if it can be shown that the parties to the marriage had no access to each other at any time when the child could have been begotten.

A1.t:
**Answer.** Conclusive proof of legitimacy can be overturned if it is proven that there was fraud, misrepresentation, or suppression of evidence at the time the proof was given.

**Why.** The law allows for the overturning of conclusive proof of legitimacy under specific conditions to ensure justice and fairness in determining parentage.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §56

A2.t:
**Answer.** Conclusive proof of legitimacy cannot be overturned under any circumstances.

**Why.** The statute explicitly states that once conclusive proof of legitimacy is established, it cannot be challenged or overturned, ensuring the finality of such determinations.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §169

A3.t:
**Answer.** The conclusive proof of legitimacy may be rebutted if it is shown that the person was not born in lawful wedlock.

**Why.** The conclusive proof of legitimacy is rebuttable if evidence is presented showing that the person was not born in lawful wedlock. This exception applies regardless of whether the person is a child or an adult.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §109

A4.t:
**Answer.** The conclusive proof of legitimacy cannot be overturned if the Court determines that, regardless of the evidence, there was sufficient evidence to justify the decision, or that the rejected evidence would not have changed the decision.

**Why.** The law provides that the improper admission or rejection of evidence does not automatically lead to a new trial or reversal of a decision. This protection applies if the Court finds that, independent of the disputed evidence, there was sufficient evidence to justify the decision, or that the rejected evidence would not have altered the decision.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §169

items.q: Under what circumstances can the list of things found and the things themselves be taken before a Magistrate having jurisdiction instead of the issuing court?
items.ref: The location must be nearer to the Magistrate having jurisdiction than to the issuing Court.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The list of things found and the things themselves can be taken before a Magistrate having jurisdiction if the issuing court is satisfied that it is in the interest of justice to do so.

**Why.** This provision allows flexibility in the judicial process, ensuring that the interests of justice are served by enabling the transfer of the case to a more appropriate or convenient court when necessary.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** When the place where the things were found is nearer to the Magistrate having jurisdiction than to the issuing court, the list and things can be taken before such Magistrate instead of the issuing court.

**Why.** This provision ensures that the convenience of the location is considered when deciding where to present the list and items found during a search, prioritizing proximity to the appropriate judicial authority.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §104

A3.t:
**Answer.** The list and the things may be taken before any Magistrate having jurisdiction if the person who received them is unable to deliver them to the issuing court.

**Why.** If the person who received the things is unable to deliver them to the issuing court, the list and the things may be taken before any Magistrate having jurisdiction.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §51

A4.t:
**Answer.** This action can occur when the search takes place outside the local jurisdiction of the issuing court, and the place where the things were found is closer to the Magistrate's jurisdiction than to the issuing court.

**Why.** The law mandates that if the search occurs outside the local jurisdiction of the issuing court, and the place where the items were found is closer to the Magistrate's jurisdiction, the list and items must be taken before the Magistrate. Furthermore, unless there is good cause to the contrary, the Magistrate must issue an order allowing the items to be taken to the issuing court.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §104

items.q: Under what circumstances can the party ask questions of its own witness that would normally be considered leading or suggestive?
items.ref: The court's discretion is required to permit the party to ask leading or suggestive questions of its own witness.

A1.t:
**Answer.** A party can ask questions of its own witness that would normally be considered leading or suggestive if the questions are necessary to clarify the testimony or to bring out particular facts.

**Why.** The rules of cross-examination allow for certain flexibility when questioning one's own witness to ensure that all relevant facts are brought to light without unduly restricting the examination.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §65

A2.t:
**Answer.** The party can ask leading or suggestive questions of its own witness in cross-examination.

**Why.** The law permits parties to ask leading questions during cross-examination, which includes asking questions that suggest the answer the examiner desires or expects, provided they are relevant to testing the witness's veracity, discovering their identity and position, or shaking their credit by injuring their character.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §149

A3.t:
**Answer.** The party may ask questions of its own witness that are not limited to those that are relevant, provided that the questions are necessary to enable the witness to give evidence in a clear and intelligible manner.

**Why.** The law permits a party to ask questions of its own witness that are not restricted to relevance if those questions are deemed necessary for the witness to provide evidence in a clear and intelligible manner.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §316

A4.t:
**Answer.** The party may ask leading questions of its own witness if the Court permits it, provided the questions are related to matters that are introductory or undisputed, or that have already been sufficiently proved.

**Why.** The law allows the party calling a witness to ask leading questions, even though these questions are prohibited during the examination-in-chief or re-examination unless the Court grants permission. This permission is granted only if the questions relate to matters that are introductory or undisputed, or if they have already been sufficiently proved.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §146

items.q: Under what circumstances is a man's conduct not considered stalking?
items.ref: If the man proves that it was pursued for the purpose of preventing or detecting crime, or was pursued under any law or to comply with any condition or requirement imposed by any person under any law, or in the particular circumstances such conduct was reasonable and justified.

A1.t:
**Answer.** A man's conduct is not considered stalking if it is carried out in a place where the accused has a reasonable expectation of being, such as their home or workplace, and the conduct is not likely to cause alarm or distress to the victim.

**Why.** The law aims to protect individuals from unwarranted harassment while respecting the rights of people to be in certain places without fear of unjustified accusations. This exception ensures that normal social interactions and activities do not fall under the ambit of stalking laws.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** Conduct shall not amount to stalking if the man who pursued it proves that it was pursued for the purpose of preventing or detecting crime and the man accused of stalking had been entrusted with the responsibility of prevention and detection of crime by the State; or it was pursued under any law or to comply with any condition or requirement imposed by any person under any law; or in the particular circumstances such conduct was reasonable and justified.

**Why.** The law provides specific exceptions to the definition of stalking, recognizing situations where the pursuit of a woman may be necessary for legitimate purposes such as crime prevention, compliance with legal requirements, or when the conduct is deemed reasonable and justified under the circumstances.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §78

A3.t:
**Answer.** A man does not commit the offense if he is acting in good faith and with reasonable grounds for believing that his conduct is necessary to prevent a crime or to protect any person from physical injury.

**Why.** The law provides an exception for actions taken in good faith and with reasonable grounds. This exception applies when the conduct is intended to prevent a crime or to protect any person from physical injury.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §145

A4.t:
**Answer.** The conduct does not amount to stalking if the man proves that it was pursued for the purpose of preventing or detecting crime and the man was entrusted with the responsibility of prevention and detection of crime by the State; or if it was pursued under any law or to comply with any condition or requirement imposed by any person under any law; or if in the particular circumstances, such conduct was reasonable and justified.

**Why.** The law provides exceptions to the definition of stalking. These exceptions apply if the man can prove that the conduct was pursued for the purpose of preventing or detecting crime and the man was entrusted with the responsibility of prevention and detection of crime by the State. Alternatively, the conduct is not stalking if it was pursued under any law or to comply with any condition or requirement imposed by any person under any law; or if in the particular circumstances, such conduct was reasonable and justified.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §78

items.q: Under what circumstances is a surety discharged from their suretyship?
items.ref: By any contract between the creditor and the principal debtor, by which the principal debtor is released, or by any act or omission of the creditor, the legal consequence of which is the discharge of the principal debtor.

A1.t:
**Answer.** A surety is discharged from their suretyship if the principal debtor discharges the debt without the consent of the surety after the surety has performed their obligation.

**Why.** The law provides that a surety is released from their liability when the principal debtor fulfills the debt without the surety's agreement, provided the surety has already fulfilled their part of the agreement.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §45

A2.t:
**Answer.** A surety is discharged from their suretyship if the creditor releases the principal debtor, omits to take action, or loses or parts with security without the surety's consent.

**Why.** The law provides that a surety can be discharged under various circumstances, including when the creditor releases the principal debtor, fails to act in a way required by the surety, or loses or relinquishes security without the surety's agreement. These provisions ensure that the surety is not held responsible beyond the original terms agreed upon.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §134

A3.t:
**Answer.** A surety is discharged if the suretyship was entered into for a specific period and that period has expired.

**Why.** The law provides that a surety is discharged when the suretyship was entered into for a certain time and that time has expired. This discharge occurs regardless of whether the suretyship was entered into for a fixed or indefinite time.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §140

A4.t:
**Answer.** A surety is discharged if the creditor releases the principal debtor through a contract, or if the creditor acts inconsistently with the surety's rights, or if the creditor loses or parts with a security without the surety's consent. A surety is also discharged if the creditor fails to enforce a remedy against the principal debtor.

**Why.** Discharge occurs when the creditor releases the principal debtor through a contract, or when the creditor acts inconsistently with the surety's rights, or when the creditor loses or parts with a security without the surety's consent. Furthermore, a surety is discharged if the creditor fails to enforce a remedy against the principal debtor.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §134

items.q: Under what circumstances is an act or offence said to be committed in consequence of abetment?
items.ref: It is committed in consequence of the instigation, or in pursuance of the conspiracy, or with the aid which constitutes the abetment.

A1.t:
**Answer.** An act or offence is said to be committed in consequence of abetment if it would not have been committed without the abetment.

**Why.** Abetment refers to the encouragement, instigation, or assistance given to another person to commit an offence. The law recognizes that certain acts or offences are directly linked to the actions of those who abet them, meaning the offence could not have occurred without the abetment.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §45

A2.t:
**Answer.** An act or offence is said to be committed in consequence of abetment when it is committed in consequence of the instigation, or in pursuance of the conspiracy, or with the aid which constitutes the abetment.

**Why.** The definition clarifies that for an act to be considered committed in consequence of abetment, it must be instigated, pursued through a conspiracy, or carried out with the aid provided during the abetment process.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §49

A3.t:
**Answer.** An act or offence is considered committed in consequence of abetment if it is done by the person who has been abetted.

**Why.** The law defines that an act or offence is committed in consequence of abetment when it is performed by the individual who was the object of the abetment.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §51

A4.t:
**Answer.** An act or offence is said to be committed in consequence of abetment when it is committed in consequence of the instigation, or in pursuance of the conspiracy, or with the aid which constitutes the abetment.

**Why.** The law defines an act or offence as committed in consequence of abetment if it occurs due to the instigation, or in pursuance of the conspiracy, or with the aid that constitutes the abetment. This definition establishes the necessary link between the abetment and the resulting act or offence.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §49

items.q: Under what circumstances is an agent liable to compensate their principal for loss or damage caused by their own neglect, want of skill, or misconduct?
items.ref: The agent is liable when the loss or damage is a direct consequence of their own neglect, want of skill, or misconduct.

A1.t:
**Answer.** An agent is liable to compensate their principal for loss or damage caused by their own neglect, want of skill, or misconduct if the agent was under a duty to exercise care, skill, or diligence in performing their duties.
