**Why.** This provision aims to protect minors who are victims of serious crimes by ensuring that the perpetrators face the full extent of the law, thereby deterring such acts against vulnerable individuals.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §156

A2.t:
**Answer.** The State Government cannot exercise its powers to remit or commute a sentence in cases involving the misappropriation or destruction of property belonging to the Central Government, or when the offence was committed by a person in the service of the Central Government while acting in their official capacity.

**Why.** These restrictions ensure that certain serious offenses related to the Central Government’s assets or officials are subject to higher scrutiny and oversight, requiring concurrence with the Central Government before any remission or commutation can be made.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §477

A3.t:
**Answer.** The State Government cannot exercise these powers if it has already exercised them in respect of the same offence.

**Why.** The power to remit or commute a sentence is subject to a limitation: the State Government cannot exercise this power if it has already exercised it for the same offence.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §451

A4.t:
**Answer.** The State Government cannot exercise these powers unless it receives concurrence from the Central Government.

**Why.** The State Government's power to remit or commute a sentence is subject to a mandatory requirement. This power can only be exercised if the State Government first obtains concurrence from the Central Government.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §477

items.q: What is the condition under which the appropriate Government may suspend the execution of a sentence?
items.ref: The appropriate Government may suspend the execution of a sentence without conditions or upon any conditions which the person sentenced accepts.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The appropriate Government may suspend the execution of a sentence if it is satisfied that there are compelling reasons to do so.

**Why.** This provision allows for flexibility in the enforcement of sentences, ensuring that the government can intervene in cases where extraordinary circumstances necessitate a suspension of the sentence's execution.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §154

A2.t:
**Answer.** The appropriate Government may suspend the execution of a sentence upon the acceptance of any conditions by the person sentenced.

**Why.** The law allows the appropriate Government to suspend the execution of a sentence subject to certain conditions that the person sentenced must accept. This provision aims to provide flexibility in the enforcement of sentences while ensuring compliance with specific terms set by the government.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §473

A3.t:
**Answer.** The appropriate Government may suspend the execution of a sentence if it is satisfied that the person has been sentenced to death or imprisonment for life.

**Why.** The power to suspend execution is triggered when the appropriate Government is satisfied that the person has been sentenced to death or imprisonment for life. This satisfaction must be made before the sentence is executed.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §451

A4.t:
**Answer.** The appropriate Government may suspend the execution of a sentence when an application is made, provided the person sentenced accepts any conditions attached to the suspension.

**Why.** The power to suspend a sentence is triggered by an application made to the appropriate Government. This application must be accepted by the person sentenced, and the suspension can only occur if the person accepts any conditions that the Government attaches to the suspension.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §473

items.q: What is the condition under which the person to whom the warrant is issued is required to execute it?
items.ref: The person for whose arrest it was issued is in, or enters on, any land or other property under his charge.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The person to whom the warrant is issued is required to execute it if the warrant is issued by a competent authority and is in accordance with the law.

**Why.** A warrant must be executed only when it is validly issued by an authorized person and adheres to the legal requirements to ensure the protection of individual rights and the proper administration of justice.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** The person to whom the warrant is issued is required to execute it if the person for whose arrest it was issued is in, or enters on, any land or other property under his charge.

**Why.** This condition ensures that the person receiving the warrant has the authority and responsibility to act upon it when the individual sought for arrest is found on their property, thereby facilitating the arrest without unnecessary delay.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §75

A3.t:
**Answer.** The person must execute the warrant if they are present in the place where the warrant was issued.

**Why.** The law mandates that the person to whom the warrant is issued must execute it if they are physically present in the place where the warrant was issued.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §74

A4.t:
**Answer.** The person must be in, or enter on, any land or other property under his charge when the warrant is issued.

**Why.** The law mandates that the person to whom the warrant is directed must be in, or enter on, any land or other property under his charge. This condition triggers the requirement for the person to acknowledge receipt of the warrant and to execute it.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §75

items.q: What is the condition under which the term of imprisonment awarded in default of payment of fine may exceed the powers of the Magistrate under section 23?
items.ref: Where imprisonment has been awarded as part of the substantive sentence.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The term of imprisonment awarded in default of payment of fine may exceed the powers of the Magistrate under section 23 if the court is a sessions court or a higher court.

**Why.** Section 23 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, limits the term of imprisonment that a magistrate can award in default of payment of fine. However, this limitation does not apply when the court has the authority to impose a longer sentence.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §23

A2.t:
**Answer.** The term of imprisonment awarded in default of payment of fine may exceed the powers of the Magistrate under section 23 if the imprisonment has already been awarded as part of the substantive sentence, and in such case, it shall not exceed one-fourth of the term of imprisonment which the Magistrate is competent to inflict as punishment for the offence otherwise than as imprisonment in default of payment of the fine.

**Why.** This condition ensures that the additional term of imprisonment awarded in default of payment does not unduly extend the total sentence beyond the Magistrate’s jurisdiction, thereby maintaining the balance between the substantive sentence and the additional penalty for non-payment of fine.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §24

A3.t:
**Answer.** The term of imprisonment awarded in default of payment of fine may exceed the powers of the Magistrate under section 23 if the Magistrate has previously passed an order under sub-section (1) of section 24.

**Why.** If a Magistrate has previously passed an order under sub-section (1) of section 24, the term of imprisonment awarded in default of payment of fine may exceed the powers of the Magistrate under section 23.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §25

A4.t:
**Answer.** The term of imprisonment awarded in default of payment of fine may exceed the powers of the Magistrate under section 23 only if the imprisonment has not already been awarded as part of the substantive sentence.

**Why.** The law allows the Court to award a term of imprisonment in default of payment of fine, provided that this term does not exceed the powers of the Magistrate under section 23. However, this limitation applies unless the imprisonment has already been awarded as part of the substantive sentence.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §24

items.q: What is the consequence for a party who calls for a document and inspects it when the producing party requires the document to be given as evidence?
items.ref: The party must give the document as evidence.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The party who calls for a document and inspects it without the producing party's consent may be deemed to have waived their right to object to the admissibility of the document at a later stage.

**Why.** This rule ensures fairness and consistency in the proceedings by preventing a party from inspecting a document and then later challenging its admissibility based on the manner of production.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** The party calling for the document is bound to give it as evidence if the producing party requires him to do so.

**Why.** This rule ensures that parties adhere to their obligations when producing documents as evidence, maintaining the integrity of the legal process by compelling the inspection and subsequent submission of relevant documents.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §166

A3.t:
**Answer.** The party calling for the document must accept the document as evidence.

**Why.** If a party calls for a document and inspects it, they are required to accept that document as evidence. This acceptance is mandatory regardless of whether the document was produced voluntarily or under compulsion.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §319

A4.t:
**Answer.** The party calling for the document must give it as evidence if the party producing it requires them to do so.

**Why.** When a party calls for a document and inspects it, they are bound to give it as evidence if the party producing it requires them to do so. This obligation applies regardless of whether the document is produced voluntarily or through a court order.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §166

items.q: What is the consequence for a person who does not appear and show cause in response to an order under section 154?
items.ref: The person shall be liable to the penalty specified in section 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The court may proceed with the trial and pass a default judgment against the absent party.

**Why.** When a party fails to appear and show cause for non-compliance with an order, the court can take the matter to its logical conclusion without the presence of that party, thereby ensuring the process of justice is not unduly delayed.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §156

A2.t:
**Answer.** He shall be liable to the penalty specified in that behalf in section 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and the order shall be made absolute.

**Why.** According to the statute, if a person against whom an order is made under section 154 does not perform the required act or appear and show cause, they will face the specified penalty and the order will be finalized.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §155

A3.t:
**Answer.** The person shall be deemed to have been convicted of the offence.

**Why.** If a person fails to appear before the Magistrate or show cause why they should not be convicted, the law deems them to have been convicted of the offence.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §228

A4.t:
**Answer.** The person shall be liable to the penalty specified in section 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, and the order shall be made absolute.

**Why.** If the person against whom an order is made under section 154 fails to perform the required act or appear and show cause, they face liability to the penalty specified in section 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. This liability triggers the order being made absolute.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §155

items.q: What is the consequence if a party fails to perform a promise at or before a specified time in a contract where time is essential?
items.ref: The contract or unperformed portion becomes voidable at the promisee's option.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The party failing to perform the promise at or before the specified time shall be liable to pay damages measured in accordance with the provisions of the contract.

**Why.** When time is of the essence in a contract, failure to perform by the stipulated time entitles the other party to claim damages without the need to wait for a reasonable time for performance.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §35

A2.t:
**Answer.** The contract, or so much of it as has not been performed, becomes voidable at the option of the promisee.

**Why.** When the parties intend that time is of the essence in their contract, the failure to perform by the specified time allows the promisee to terminate the contract or treat the unperformed part of the contract as voidable. This ensures that the critical timing agreed upon by both parties is strictly adhered to, reflecting their mutual understanding and agreement on the importance of timely performance.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §55

A3.t:
**Answer.** The party who fails to perform the promise at or before the specified time shall be liable to pay damages.

**Why.** If a party fails to perform the promise at or before the time fixed for its performance, that party shall be liable to pay damages.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §50

A4.t:
**Answer.** The contract, or the part that has not been performed, becomes voidable at the option of the promisee.

**Why.** If the parties intended that time was of the essence, the failure to perform the promise at the specified time renders the contract voidable. This voidability is specifically tied to the promisee's option.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §55

items.q: What is the consequence if a party fails to perform a promise at or before a specified time in a contract where time is not essential?
items.ref: The contract does not become voidable, but the promisee is entitled to compensation for any loss occasioned by the failure.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The party who fails to perform the promise at or before the specified time shall be liable to pay damages for non-performance of the contract.

**Why.** When time is of the essence in a contract, failure to perform by the stipulated date entitles the other party to claim damages as a remedy.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §35

A2.t:
**Answer.** The contract does not become voidable by the failure to perform the promise at the specified time; however, the promisee is entitled to compensation from the promisor for any loss occasioned to him by such failure.

**Why.** When the intention of the parties is not that time should be of the essence of the contract, the failure to perform the promise at the specified time does not render the entire contract voidable. Instead, the promisee can seek compensation for any losses incurred due to the promisor's failure to perform.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §55

A3.t:
**Answer.** The party who fails to perform the promise at or before the specified time shall be liable to pay damages.

**Why.** If a party fails to perform a promise at or before the time fixed for performance, and that time is not essential, the law mandates that the party must pay damages.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §49

A4.t:
**Answer.** The contract does not become voidable by the failure to perform the promise at the specified time. However, the promisee is entitled to compensation from the promisor for any loss occasioned to him by such failure.

**Why.** If the intention of the parties was not that time should be of the essence of the contract, the contract does not become voidable by the failure to perform the promise at the specified time. Nevertheless, the promisee retains the right to receive compensation from the promisor for any loss that the promisee suffers due to this failure.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §55

items.q: What is the consequence if a person fails to comply with a conditional order to remove an obstruction or nuisance?
items.ref: The order may be made absolute.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The person may be imprisoned for a term which may extend to six months or with a fine, or with both.

**Why.** When a person is directed to remove an obstruction or nuisance within a specified period and fails to do so, they are subject to criminal contempt of court and can be punished accordingly.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §95

A2.t:
**Answer.** The person may be arrested by any police officer without warrant and will be produced before the District Magistrate.

**Why.** The statute provides that if a person fails to comply with a conditional order to remove an obstruction or nuisance, the District Magistrate can order the person to be arrested and brought before them.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §152

A3.t:
**Answer.** The person shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, and they are also liable to a fine.

**Why.** If a person fails to remove the obstruction or nuisance within the time specified in the order, they face punishment with simple imprisonment up to six months, along with a fine.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §289

A4.t:
**Answer.** The person who caused the obstruction or nuisance may be arrested by any police officer without warrant and must then be produced before the District Magistrate.

**Why.** If a person fails to comply with a conditional order to remove an obstruction or nuisance, the person who caused the obstruction or nuisance can be arrested by any police officer without warrant. This arrest action requires the person to be subsequently produced before the District Magistrate.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §152

items.q: What is the consequence if a person whose acts were done without their knowledge or authority ratifies those acts?
items.ref: The same effects will follow as if they had been performed by their authority.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The ratification by a person whose acts were done without their knowledge or authority has no legal consequence and does not validate the acts.

**Why.** Ratification is not necessary for an act to be binding if the person was unaware or lacked authority at the time of the act. The law aims to protect individuals from being bound by actions they did not consent to or were unaware of.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §56

A2.t:
**Answer.** The person may elect to ratify or disown such acts. If ratified, the acts will have the same effects as if they had been performed with authority.

**Why.** When a person's acts are done without their knowledge or authority, they can choose to either acknowledge and accept the consequences of those acts (ratify them) or reject them (disown them). If the person decides to ratify the acts, the legal implications become equivalent to if the acts had been performed with explicit authorization.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §196

A3.t:
**Answer.** The acts become valid and binding on the person who ratified them.

**Why.** If a person does an act without their knowledge or authority, and subsequently ratifies that act, the law deems the act to be valid and binding on the person who ratified it.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §194

A4.t:
**Answer.** The person may elect to ratify or disown the acts. If the person elects to ratify the acts, the same legal consequences apply as if the acts had been done with the person's authority.

**Why.** The law provides that when acts are done without a person's knowledge or authority, the person has the option to ratify or disown these acts. If the person chooses to ratify, the legal consequences are identical to those that would have occurred if the acts had been done with the person's authority.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §196

items.q: What is the consequence if someone offers or attempts to offer resistance to the recapture of a State prisoner or prisoner of war who has escaped from lawful custody?
items.ref: imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine

A1.t:
**Answer.** The person offering or attempting to offer resistance shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years, or with a fine, or with both.

**Why.** This provision aims to deter any form of interference with the process of recapturing a prisoner who has escaped from lawful custody, ensuring the safety and security of such individuals while they are being returned to custody.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §154

A2.t:
**Answer.** Whoever knowingly aids or assists a State prisoner or prisoner of war in escaping from lawful custody, or rescues or attempts to rescue such a prisoner, or harbours or conceals such a prisoner who has escaped from lawful custody, or offers or attempts to offer any resistance to the recapture of such prisoner, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.

**Why.** This provision outlines the severe penalties for aiding, assisting, or obstructing the recapture of a State prisoner or prisoner of war who has escaped from lawful custody. The intent behind this rule is to ensure the safe and secure custody of prisoners to maintain public order and national security.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §158

A3.t:
**Answer.** The person shall be punished with imprisonment for a term that may extend up to ten years, and they are also liable to a fine.

**Why.** The law mandates that anyone who offers or attempts to offer resistance to the recapture of such a prisoner shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and they are also liable to a fine.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §154

A4.t:
**Answer.** The person shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.

**Why.** The law mandates that anyone who knowingly aids or assists a State prisoner or prisoner of war in escaping from lawful custody, or who offers or attempts to offer resistance to the recapture of such a prisoner, shall face severe punishment. This penalty includes imprisonment for life or up to ten years, along with liability to fine.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §158

items.q: What is the consequence if sufficient security is not given when a person is required to give security to appear before a Magistrate?
items.ref: The person will be forwarded in custody to the Magistrate.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The person may be committed to prison for a term not exceeding three months or with a fine not exceeding one thousand rupees, or with both.

**Why.** When a person is required to give security to appear before a Magistrate and fails to provide the necessary security, the court may impose an alternative penalty to ensure the person appears as required.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** The person will be committed to prison until such period expires or until within such period he gives the security to the Court or Magistrate who made the order requiring it.

**Why.** The statute mandates that if a person ordered to give security fails to do so, they will be detained in prison until they comply with the order or the period expires. This ensures that individuals who are required to provide security for their appearance before a Magistrate are held accountable for their obligations.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §141

A3.t:
**Answer.** The person shall be committed to jail for a period not exceeding seven days.

**Why.** If the person fails to furnish sufficient security, they shall be committed to jail for a term not exceeding seven days. This commitment is mandatory upon the failure of security.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §105

A4.t:
**Answer.** The person must be committed to prison or detained in prison until the period for which security was required expires, or until they provide the security to the Court or Magistrate who made the order.

**Why.** If a person fails to give security on the required date, they face imprisonment or detention in prison. This applies whether the person is already in prison or is required to be detained in prison. The duration of the detention is tied to the period for which the security was originally required.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §141

items.q: What is the consequence if the State Government makes an order of suspension, remission, or commutation of sentences for a person who has been convicted of offences that relate to matters to which the executive power of the Union extends?
items.ref: The State Government's order will not have effect unless a similar order has also been made by the Central Government with regard to the offences that relate to matters to which the executive power of the Union extends.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The State Government's order of suspension, remission, or commutation of sentences for such offences requires approval from the Union Government.

**Why.** Such orders pertain to matters under the executive power of the Union, thus requiring central approval to ensure uniformity and consistency in the application of laws across the nation.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §154

A2.t:
**Answer.** The order of suspension, remission, or commutation of sentences will not have effect unless an order for the same has also been made by the Central Government.

**Why.** This ensures that the Central Government concurs in the decision to suspend, remit, or commute a sentence when the offences relate to matters under its executive power, thereby maintaining a level of oversight and coordination between the state and central governments.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §477

A3.t:
**Answer.** The order made by the State Government shall be deemed to have been made under section 451.

**Why.** If the State Government makes an order of suspension, remission, or commutation of sentences for a person convicted of offences relating to matters to which the executive power of the Union extends, such order shall be deemed to have been made under section 451.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §452

A4.t:
**Answer.** The order of suspension, remission, or commutation of sentences cannot take effect unless the Central Government has also made an order concerning the same offences.

**Why.** The power of the State Government to suspend, remit, or commute sentences is subject to a mandatory requirement. This requirement mandates that the Central Government must first issue an order regarding the specific offences committed by the person, particularly those related to matters to which the executive power of the Union extends.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §477

items.q: What is the consequence if the person attempting to commit the offence fails in the attempt because of circumstances beyond their control?
items.ref: The person is still guilty under this section.

A1.t:
**Answer.** There is no punishment for an attempted offence if the attempt fails due to circumstances beyond the person's control.

**Why.** The law does not consider an attempt to commit an offence as punishable when the failure to complete the offence is due to factors beyond the individual's control, as it would be unjust to penalize such attempts.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §45

A2.t:
**Answer.** The person attempting to commit the offence is still guilty under the law.

**Why.** The law provides that anyone who attempts to commit an offence and does any act towards its commission remains guilty even if they fail due to circumstances beyond their control. This ensures that attempts at committing offences are discouraged and punished accordingly.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §62

A3.t:
**Answer.** The person shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and they are also liable to a fine.

**Why.** If the person fails in the attempt due to circumstances beyond their control, the punishment is imprisonment up to ten years, along with liability to a fine.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §145

A4.t:
**Answer.** The person is still considered guilty of the attempt, even if they fail due to circumstances beyond their control.

**Why.** The law establishes that whoever attempts to commit an offence punishable by this Sanhita with imprisonment for life or imprisonment, or to cause such an offence to be committed, and in such attempt does any act towards the commission of the offence, shall be guilty of the attempt. This guilt remains established regardless of whether the person fails in the attempt due to circumstances beyond their control.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §62

items.q: What is the consequence if the person from whom security was demanded fails to furnish fresh security after a surety becomes insolvent or dies, or a bond is forfeited?
items.ref: The Court or Magistrate may proceed as if there had been a default in complying with the original order.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The person from whom security was demanded shall be liable to pay the amount secured within six months from the date when the demand for furnishing fresh security was made.

**Why.** This provision ensures that the obligation to secure an amount remains enforceable even when the original surety is no longer available, thus safeguarding the interests of the creditor.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §45

A2.t:
**Answer.** The Court by whose order such bond was taken, or a Magistrate of the first class may proceed as if there had been a default in complying with such original order.

**Why.** When a surety becomes insolvent or dies, or a bond is forfeited, the law allows the Court or a Magistrate to treat it as a default in compliance with the original order, leading to potential further action against the principal debtor.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §493

A3.t:
**Answer.** The person must be detained in custody until they provide fresh security.

**Why.** If the person fails to furnish fresh security within the time limit, they shall be detained in custody until such security is furnished.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §495

A4.t:
**Answer.** The Court or Magistrate may proceed as if there had been a default in complying with the original order.

**Why.** If the person from whom security was demanded does not furnish fresh security, the Court or Magistrate may proceed as if there had been a default in complying with the original order.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §493

items.q: What is the consequence of a person being born during the continuance of a valid marriage between their mother and a man, or within 280 days after the dissolution of that marriage, if the mother remains unmarried?
items.ref: This is considered conclusive proof that the person is the legitimate child of that man.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The child is deemed to be legitimate.

**Why.** This rule ensures that the child born under these circumstances is treated as legitimate, thereby protecting the rights of the child and ensuring that they can inherit property and enjoy other legal rights accorded to legitimate children.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §25

A2.t:
**Answer.** The fact that any person was born during the continuance of a valid marriage between his mother and any man, or within two hundred and eighty days after its dissolution, the mother remaining unmarried, shall be conclusive proof that he is the legitimate child of that man, unless it can be shown that the parties to the marriage had no access to each other at any time when he could have been begotten.

**Why.** This rule provides a presumption of legitimacy for children born under specified circumstances, which simplifies the burden of proof for establishing paternity. It is designed to protect the rights of the child and the presumed father without requiring additional evidence unless there is clear evidence to the contrary.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §116

A3.t:
**Answer.** The child shall be deemed to have been begotten by the husband of the mother.

**Why.** If a child is born while the mother is married to a man, or within 280 days after the dissolution of such marriage, and the mother is not subsequently married, the law deems the child to have been begotten by the husband of the mother.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §159

A4.t:
**Answer.** The person is conclusively presumed to be the legitimate child of that man, unless it can be proven that the parties to the marriage had no access to each other at any time when the child could have been conceived.

**Why.** The law establishes that if a child is born during the continuation of a valid marriage or within 280 days after its dissolution, the child is presumed to be the legitimate child of the man, unless evidence proves otherwise.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §116

items.q: What is the consequence of a person failing to perform the act directed by the order within the time fixed?
items.ref: The Magistrate may cause it to be performed and recover the costs of performing it.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The person may be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to three months or with fine or with both.

**Why.** When a person fails to comply with an order within the stipulated time, the law provides for a punitive measure to ensure compliance, which includes imprisonment, a financial penalty, or both, to enforce the order.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §154

A2.t:
**Answer.** The person may be liable to the penalty provided by section 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.

**Why.** If a person fails to perform the act directed by the order within the time fixed, they can be held responsible for the consequences outlined in section 223, which includes penalties such as simple imprisonment or fines.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §160

A3.t:
**Answer.** The person shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with a fine, or with both.

**Why.** If the person fails to perform the act within the time fixed, they shall be punished with imprisonment for a term extending up to six months, or with a fine, or with both.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §169

A4.t:
**Answer.** The Magistrate may cause the act to be performed and may recover the costs of performing it, either by the sale of any building, goods, or other property removed by his order, or by the distress and sale of any other movable property of the person within or without the Magistrate's local jurisdiction.

**Why.** If the person against whom the order was made fails to perform the act within the time fixed, the Magistrate has the power to cause the act to be performed. This action allows the Magistrate to recover the costs associated with the performance, which can be recovered through the sale of property or through distress and sale of movable property.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §160

items.q: What is the consequence of a person's fraudulent acceptance or receipt of property knowing they have no right to it?
items.ref: The person shall be punished with imprisonment or fine, or both.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The person is liable to return the property to its rightful owner and may be punished with imprisonment for a term which may be extendable to six months or with a fine, or with both.

**Why.** This provision aims to deter fraud and ensure the restoration of property to its rightful owner. It imposes a duty on individuals to act honestly and with due regard to the rights of others.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §45

A2.t:
**Answer.** The person shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

**Why.** The statute specifically addresses the act of fraudulently accepting or receiving property when the individual knows they have no right to it. This offense is considered a criminal act and is subject to penalties including imprisonment and/or fines.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §244

A3.t:
**Answer.** The person shall be punished with imprisonment for a term that may extend up to seven years, and they must also be liable to a fine.

**Why.** The law mandates punishment with imprisonment up to seven years, along with liability to a fine. This penalty applies when a person fraudulently accepts or receives property knowing they do not have the right to it.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §315

A4.t:
**Answer.** The person shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both.

**Why.** The law mandates punishment for anyone who fraudulently accepts, receives, or claims property or an interest in property, knowing they have no right to it, or who practices deception regarding rights to property, intending to prevent the property from being taken as a forfeiture or in satisfaction of a fine, or from being taken in execution of a decree or order.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §244

items.q: What is the consequence of knowingly or negligently conveying a person by water in an unsafe or overloaded vessel?
items.ref: The offender shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The person conveying the vessel can be punished with imprisonment up to six months or a fine, or both.

**Why.** This provision aims to ensure the safety of passengers transported by water and to penalize those who compromise this safety through negligence or intentional actions.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** The person conveying a person by water in an unsafe or overloaded vessel shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.

**Why.** This provision aims to ensure the safety of passengers by penalizing those who knowingly or negligently operate vessels in a hazardous condition, thus deterring such practices and protecting public safety.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §284

A3.t:
**Answer.** The person shall be punished with imprisonment for a term that may extend to two years, and they are also liable to a fine.

**Why.** The law mandates punishment with imprisonment up to two years, along with a fine, if the person knowingly or negligently conveys another person by water using a vessel that is unsafe or overloaded.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §279

A4.t:
**Answer.** The offender shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term up to six months, or with a fine up to five thousand rupees, or with both.

**Why.** The law mandates punishment for whoever knowingly or negligently conveys a person by water in a vessel that is in a state or so loaded as to endanger the life of that person. This offense carries a penalty of imprisonment up to six months, or a fine up to five thousand rupees, or both.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §284

items.q: What is the consequence of pulling down, repairing, or constructing a building without taking measures to guard against probable danger to human life from the fall of that building?
items.ref: Punishment with imprisonment or fine, or both

A1.t:
**Answer.** The person responsible may be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year or with a fine, or with both.

**Why.** This provision aims to ensure public safety by mandating necessary precautions before any construction or alteration work is undertaken. Failure to do so can lead to potential hazards and thus attracts criminal liability.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** The person will be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both.

**Why.** The statute mandates that anyone involved in construction activities must take necessary precautions to prevent potential hazards to human life. Failure to do so results in criminal liability.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §290

A3.t:
**Answer.** The person shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, and they are also liable to a fine.

**Why.** The law mandates that any person who pulls down, repairs, or constructs a building must take all necessary measures to guard against probable danger to human life from the fall of that building. Failure to do so results in punishment with imprisonment up to two years, along with liability to a fine.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §291

A4.t:
**Answer.** The person shall be punished with imprisonment up to six months, or with a fine up to five thousand rupees, or with both.

**Why.** The law mandates punishment for anyone who, while performing construction, repair, or demolition, fails to take measures sufficient to guard against probable danger to human life from the fall of the building or its parts. This failure results in a penalty of imprisonment up to six months, or a fine up to five thousand rupees, or both.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §290

items.q: What is the consequence of repeatedly following a woman and contacting her despite her clear indication of disinterest?
items.ref: The man commits the offence of stalking.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The person may be punished with imprisonment for a term which may be extended to three months or with a fine, or with both.

**Why.** This provision aims to protect individuals from harassment and stalking. Repeatedly following a woman and contacting her despite her clear indication of disinterest is considered a form of harassment and can lead to criminal charges under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §56

A2.t:
**Answer.** The person commits the offence of stalking.

**Why.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, explicitly defines stalking as the repeated following and contacting of a woman despite her clear indication of disinterest. The act is punishable with imprisonment and a fine.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §78

A3.t:
**Answer.** The person shall be punished with imprisonment for a term that may extend to two years, or with a fine, or with both.

**Why.** The law mandates punishment for anyone who repeatedly follows or contacts a woman after she has expressed a desire not to be followed or contacted. This offense carries a penalty of imprisonment up to two years, or a fine, or both.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §145

A4.t:
**Answer.** The offender shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine. If the offense is repeated, the punishment increases to imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and the offender remains liable to fine.

**Why.** The law defines stalking as an offense committed by a man who repeatedly contacts a woman despite her clear indication of disinterest. The initial penalty for this offense is imprisonment up to three years and a fine. If the offense is repeated, the penalty escalates to imprisonment up to five years and a fine.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §78

items.q: What is the consequence of the buyer's failure to pay the price at the time fixed?
items.ref: The contract is subject to rescission.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The buyer is liable to pay interest at the rate specified in the contract from the date when the price became due.

**Why.** The law aims to ensure that the seller is compensated for the delay in payment by the buyer, thereby maintaining the integrity of contractual obligations and providing a fair remedy for the seller.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** The seller has the right to rescind the contract and retain the goods.

**Why.** When the buyer fails to pay the price at the time fixed, the seller can terminate the contract and keep the goods as a remedy. This ensures that the seller is not left without recourse for non-payment.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §121

A3.t:
**Answer.** The seller has the right to retain the goods until the price is paid.

**Why.** If the buyer fails to pay the price at the time fixed, the seller retains the right to retain the goods. This retention right is triggered when the buyer does not make the payment on the agreed-upon date.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §95

A4.t:
**Answer.** The seller has the right to rescind the contract and claim compensation for any trouble or expense incurred by the seller.

**Why.** When the buyer fails to pay the price at the time fixed, the seller has the right to rescind the contract. Furthermore, the seller is entitled to claim compensation for any trouble or expense that the seller has incurred in consequence of the failure to pay the price.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §121

items.q: What is the consequence of the creditor's omission to supply necessary timber in a contract where the creditor guaranteed the principal debtor's performance?
items.ref: The surety is discharged from their suretyship.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The principal debtor is discharged from the obligation under the contract.

**Why.** When the creditor, who has guaranteed the principal debtor's performance, fails to provide the necessary timber as agreed, it constitutes a breach of the contract terms, thereby releasing the principal debtor from their obligations.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §56

A2.t:
**Answer.** C is discharged from his suretyship.

**Why.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §134 states that the surety is discharged if the creditor omits to do any act which his duty to the surety requires him to do, and this omission impairs the surety's eventual remedy against the principal debtor. In this case, the omission to supply necessary timber by the creditor (B) impairs C's ability to seek remedy from the principal debtor (A).

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §134

A3.t:
**Answer.** The creditor must pay the price of the timber that was not supplied.

**Why.** If the creditor fails to supply the timber, the creditor is required to pay the price of the timber that was not supplied. This payment obligation arises when the creditor has guaranteed the performance of the principal debtor.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §149

A4.t:
**Answer.** The surety is discharged from liability because the creditor's omission to supply the necessary timber is an act that discharges the principal debtor.

**Why.** The law provides that if the creditor omits to do any act required by his duty to the surety, and this omission impairs the surety's remedy against the principal debtor, the surety is discharged. In the example, the creditor B omitted to supply the necessary timber, which is an act that discharges the principal debtor.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §134

items.q: What is the consequence when a Judge or Magistrate ceases to exercise jurisdiction in a case and is succeeded by another Judge or Magistrate?
items.ref: The succeeding Judge or Magistrate may act on the evidence recorded by their predecessor, or partly recorded by their predecessor and partly recorded by themselves.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The proceedings in the case shall continue under the new Judge or Magistrate who succeeds the previous one.

**Why.** This ensures continuity in judicial proceedings and prevents any disruption in the course of justice when there is a change in the presiding officer.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §154

A2.t:
**Answer.** The succeeding Judge or Magistrate may act on the evidence recorded by the previous Judge or Magistrate, provided they believe further examination of any witness is necessary for justice.

**Why.** This rule allows continuity in the judicial process by permitting the new Judge or Magistrate to utilize the evidence already recorded, while ensuring that justice is not compromised by allowing further examination of witnesses when deemed necessary.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §365

A3.t:
**Answer.** The proceedings in that case shall be deemed to have been stayed until the succeeding Judge or Magistrate has had an opportunity of examining the record.

**Why.** If a Judge or Magistrate ceases to exercise jurisdiction in any case, and is succeeded by another Judge or Magistrate, the proceedings in that case shall be deemed to have been stayed until the succeeding Judge or Magistrate has had an opportunity of examining the record.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §491

A4.t:
**Answer.** The succeeding Judge or Magistrate may act on the evidence recorded by the predecessor, or partly recorded by the predecessor and partly recorded by himself. If the succeeding Judge or Magistrate believes further examination of any witness is necessary, they may resummon that witness and conduct the required examination.

**Why.** The law provides that when a Judge or Magistrate ceases to exercise jurisdiction and is succeeded by another Judge or Magistrate, the succeeding Judge or Magistrate can act on the evidence recorded by the predecessor. Furthermore, if the succeeding Judge or Magistrate determines that further examination of any witness is necessary, they have the power to resummon that witness and conduct the examination.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §365

items.q: What is the consequence when the promisor of the promise last mentioned fails to perform it in a contract consisting of reciprocal promises?
items.ref: The promisor cannot claim the performance of the reciprocal promise and must make compensation to the other party for any loss sustained.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The promisee may treat the contract as discharged and be relieved of the obligation to perform their part of the contract.

**Why.** When a contract involves reciprocal promises and the promisor fails to perform their obligation, the promisee is entitled to terminate the contract and no longer has a duty to fulfill their side of the agreement.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §26

A2.t:
**Answer.** The promisor cannot claim the performance of the reciprocal promise and must make compensation to the other party for any loss sustained due to the non-performance of the contract.

**Why.** This rule applies when the contract involves reciprocal promises where the performance of one promise is contingent on the performance of another. If the promisor of the last mentioned promise fails to perform, the contract becomes voidable for the other party, who can seek compensation for any losses incurred.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §54

A3.t:
**Answer.** The promisor must perform the promise that was due from him.

**Why.** If the promisor of the promise last mentioned fails to perform it, he must perform the promise that was due from him. This rule applies specifically when the contract consists of reciprocal promises.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §50

A4.t:
**Answer.** The promisor cannot claim the performance of the reciprocal promise and must make compensation to the other party for any loss sustained due to the non-performance of the contract.

**Why.** If a contract consists of reciprocal promises and one of those promises cannot be performed, or its performance cannot be claimed until the other has been performed, and the promisor of the last mentioned promise fails to perform it, the promisor loses the right to claim performance of the reciprocal promise. Furthermore, the promisor must compensate the other party for any loss suffered due to the non-performance of the contract.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §54

items.q: What is the effect of a creditor releasing one co-surety on the other co-sureties?
items.ref: The release does not discharge the others.

A1.t:
**Answer.** A creditor releasing one co-surety discharges all the other co-sureties from their liability.

**Why.** When a surety agreement involves multiple co-sureties, releasing one of them from their obligation effectively extinguishes the entire guarantee, thereby discharging all the remaining co-sureties from their respective liabilities.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §65

A2.t:
**Answer.** A release by the creditor of one of the co-sureties does not discharge the others; neither does it free the surety so released from his responsibility to the other sureties.

**Why.** This rule ensures that the burden of the debt remains shared among all co-sureties, maintaining the balance of responsibility even after the release of one of them.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §138

A3.t:
**Answer.** The release of one co-surety discharges all the others from their liability.

**Why.** When a creditor releases one co-surety, the law dictates that this action discharges all the remaining co-sureties from their liability.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §145

A4.t:
**Answer.** The release of one co-surety does not discharge the others, nor does it free the released surety from his responsibility to the remaining co-sureties.

**Why.** The law dictates that the release of one co-surety does not discharge the others. Furthermore, the released surety remains responsible to the other co-sureties for the entire debt.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §138

items.q: What is the effect of a notification, proclamation, power, form, or local jurisdiction that was in force immediately before the commencement of this Sanhita?
items.ref: It shall be deemed to have been published, issued, conferred, specified, defined, passed, or made under the corresponding provisions of this Sanhita.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The notification, proclamation, power, form, or local jurisdiction that was in force immediately before the commencement of this Sanhita continues to be in force until modified or repealed by subsequent notification, proclamation, or enactment.

**Why.** This provision ensures continuity and stability in the application of laws and procedures during the transition period following the commencement of the new legal framework.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §5

A2.t:
**Answer.** Such notifications, proclamations, powers, forms, and local jurisdictions shall be deemed to have been published, issued, conferred, specified, defined, passed, or made under the corresponding provisions of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.

**Why.** The provisions of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, continue the validity of certain actions taken under the repealed Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, ensuring continuity in the administration of justice.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Sursha Sanhita, 2023, §531

A3.t:
**Answer.** Such notification, proclamation, power, form, or local jurisdiction shall continue to be in force until it is repealed or amended by subsequent law.

**Why.** The law ensures that any notification, proclamation, power, form, or local jurisdiction that was in force immediately before the commencement of this Sanhita continues to remain in force. This continuity applies unless and until such notification, proclamation, power, form, or local jurisdiction is repealed or amended by subsequent law.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §519

A4.t:
**Answer.** Such notification, proclamation, power, form, or local jurisdiction shall be deemed to have been published, issued, conferred, specified, defined, passed, or made under the corresponding provisions of this Sanhita.

**Why.** The law provides that any notification, proclamation, power, form, or local jurisdiction that was in force immediately before the commencement of this Sanhita shall be deemed to have been published, issued, conferred, specified, defined, passed, or made under the corresponding provisions of this Sanhita.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §531

items.q: What is the effect of a party producing a document that was previously called for and inspected by the other party?
items.ref: The party calling for the document must give it as evidence.

A1.t:
**Answer.** A party producing a document that was previously called for and inspected by the other party is deemed to have admitted the authenticity of the document.

**Why.** When a document has been previously called for and inspected, it is presumed that both parties acknowledge its authenticity, and producing it again is considered an admission of its validity.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** The party producing the document is entitled to have it admitted as evidence if the other party requires it.

**Why.** When a party has already called for and inspected a document, they are under an obligation to provide it as evidence upon request from the other party, as per the statute.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §166

A3.t:
**Answer.** The party who produced the document is not entitled to any expenses incurred in producing it.

**Why.** If a party produces a document that was previously called for and inspected by the other party, that party is not entitled to any expenses incurred in producing it.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §319

A4.t:
**Answer.** The party who called for the document is bound to give it as evidence if the party producing it requires him to do so.

**Why.** When a party calls for a document that he has given notice to produce, and that document is produced and inspected by the party calling for it, the law mandates that the party who called for the document must provide it as evidence if the party producing it requires it.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §166

items.q: What is the effect of a statement in writing by the Court issuing the proclamation stating that it was published on a specified day?
items.ref: It is conclusive evidence that the requirements of the section have been complied with and that the proclamation was published on that day.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The statement in writing by the Court is taken to be proof of publication on the specified day.

**Why.** The Court's written statement regarding the date of publication is considered conclusive evidence of the actual date of publication, ensuring that the legal process can proceed based on a verified date.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §45

A2.t:
**Answer.** The statement in writing by the Court issuing the proclamation is conclusive evidence that the proclamation was published on the specified day.

**Why.** This rule ensures that the publication of the proclamation is taken as fact once the Court makes a written statement to that effect, streamlining the process and reducing the burden of proof for compliance with the publication requirement.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §84(3)

A3.t:
**Answer.** The statement in writing by the Court is conclusive proof that the proclamation was published on the date stated.

**Why.** The statement in writing by the Court is conclusive proof that the proclamation was published on the date stated.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §159

A4.t:
**Answer.** The statement in writing by the Court is conclusive evidence that the proclamation was published on the specified day, and that it was published in the manner specified in clause (i) of sub-section (2).

**Why.** The statement in writing by the Court is conclusive evidence that the proclamation was published on the specified day, and that it was published in the manner specified in clause (i) of sub-section (2).

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §84

items.q: What is the effect of the mother's remarriage within 280 days after the dissolution of the previous marriage on the legitimacy of a child born during this period?
items.ref: The mother's remarriage within 280 days does not affect the legitimacy of the child.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The child remains legitimate.

**Why.** The law does not revoke the legitimacy of a child born during the subsistence of a valid marriage, regardless of the mother's subsequent remarriage within a certain period.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §154

A2.t:
**Answer.** The child's legitimacy remains conclusive proof of the father's paternity unless it can be shown that the parties had no access during the period.

**Why.** The statute explicitly states that the birth of a child during the mother's subsequent marriage within 280 days of the dissolution of the previous marriage does not affect the legitimacy of the child, provided there is no evidence of lack of access.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §116

A3.t:
**Answer.** The child is not considered legitimate.

**Why.** If the mother remarries within 280 days after the dissolution of her previous marriage, the law deems that no child born to her during that period shall be deemed legitimate.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §159

A4.t:
**Answer.** The fact that the child was born during the continuance of the marriage or within 280 days after its dissolution, while the mother remained unmarried, is conclusive proof that the child is the legitimate child of the man, unless it can be shown that the parties to the marriage had no access to each other at any time when the child could have been begotten.

**Why.** The law establishes that the birth of a child during the continuance of a valid marriage or within 280 days after its dissolution, while the mother remains unmarried, is conclusive proof of legitimacy. This presumption holds unless evidence is presented showing that the parties to the marriage did not have access to each other at any time when the child could have been begotten.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §116

items.q: What is the effect of the parties' agreement to substitute a new contract for the original one?
items.ref: The original contract need not be performed.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The agreement to substitute a new contract for the original one discharges the obligation under the original contract.

**Why.** When parties agree to substitute a new contract for an existing one, the original contract is discharged, and the new contract becomes binding between the parties. This discharge extinguishes the rights and obligations under the old contract, and the new contract takes its place.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §61

A2.t:
**Answer.** The original contract need not be performed, and a new contract is formed.

**Why.** When the parties agree to substitute a new contract for the original one, or to rescind or alter the original contract, the original contract is terminated, and a new one is created in its place. This agreement effectively extinguishes the original obligation and creates a new one.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §62

A3.t:
**Answer.** The original contract is discharged, and the substituted contract takes its place.

**Why.** When the parties agree to substitute a new contract, the original contract is discharged. This discharge means that the new contract becomes the operative agreement between the parties.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §59

A4.t:
**Answer.** The original contract is extinguished, and a new contract is formed.

**Why.** If the parties agree to substitute a new contract for the existing one, or to rescind or alter it, the original contract ceases to exist. This action results in the formation of a new contract.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §62

items.q: What is the extent of liability of an abettor when the act abetted causes a different effect from that intended by the abettor?
items.ref: The abettor is liable to the same extent as if he had abetted the act with the intention of causing that effect.

A1.t:
**Answer.** An abettor is liable for the effect caused by the principal offender, whether or not it was the effect intended by the abettor.

**Why.** The liability of an abettor is based on the principle that an abettor is responsible for all acts committed in furtherance of the crime, regardless of the specific intent behind the abettor’s involvement.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §45

A2.t:
**Answer.** The abettor is liable for the effect caused, in the same manner and to the same extent as if he had abetted the act with the intention of causing that effect, provided he knew that the act abetted was likely to cause that effect.

**Why.** This rule ensures that an abettor remains accountable for the consequences of their actions, even if the outcome differs from what they initially intended. It aligns the liability of the abettor with the actual result of the abetted act, promoting fairness and justice.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §53

A3.t:
**Answer.** The abettor is liable for the effect which he intended to cause, and also for any other effect which was caused by the act.

**Why.** An abettor is liable for the effect which he intended to cause, and also for any other effect which was caused by the act. This liability applies even if the act abetted causes a different effect from that intended by the abettor.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §51

A4.t:
**Answer.** The abettor is liable for the effect caused, in the same manner and to the same extent as if he had abetted the act with the intention of causing that effect, provided he knew that the act abetted was likely to cause that effect.

**Why.** If an act is abetted with the intention of causing a specific effect, but the act actually causes a different effect, the abettor remains liable. This liability applies only if the abettor knew that the act abetted was likely to cause the effect that was actually caused.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §53

items.q: What is the extent of the jurisdiction and powers of every Magistrate appointed under section 9 or section 11, except as otherwise provided by definition?
items.ref: Throughout the district

A1.t:
**Answer.** Every Magistrate appointed under section 9 or section 11 has jurisdiction over all offences within the local limits of his jurisdiction and shall have the powers necessary to be exercised in connection with such jurisdiction.

**Why.** This provision ensures that Magistrates appointed under specific sections have comprehensive authority over the areas they oversee, enabling them to handle all related matters effectively without additional limitations.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §95

A2.t:
**Answer.** The jurisdiction and powers of every Magistrate appointed under section 9 or section 11 extend throughout the district, unless otherwise provided by a definition made by the Chief Judicial Magistrate.

**Why.** This rule ensures that Magistrates appointed under sections 9 or 11 have a broad jurisdiction within their district, but allows for specific limitations to be set by the Chief Judicial Magistrate through a defined local limit.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §12

A3.t:
**Answer.** Every such Magistrate has jurisdiction throughout the district where they are appointed, and they have all the powers that a Magistrate of the first class would have in that district.

**Why.** The law grants every Magistrate appointed under section 9 or section 11 jurisdiction throughout the district where they are appointed. Furthermore, these Magistrates are granted all the powers that a Magistrate of the first class would possess within that district.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §14

A4.t:
**Answer.** The jurisdiction and powers of every such Magistrate shall extend throughout the district.

**Why.** The jurisdiction and powers of every Magistrate appointed under section 9 or section 11 shall extend throughout the district, unless the context otherwise requires.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §12

items.q: What is the general rule regarding the admissibility of confessions made to police officers?
items.ref: No confession made to a police officer shall be proved as against a person accused of any offence.

A1.t:
**Answer.** Confessions made to police officers are generally not admissible in evidence.

**Why.** This rule aims to prevent police coercion and ensure fair trials by disallowing statements that may have been obtained under duress.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** Confessions made to police officers are generally not admissible in court.

**Why.** This rule aims to prevent coerced or unreliable statements from being used against an accused. The confession must either be made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate or not while the accused is in police custody, unless certain conditions are met.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §23

A3.t:
**Answer.** Confessions made to police officers are generally not admissible in evidence.

**Why.** The law stipulates that no confession made to a police officer shall be deemed to be relevant unless it falls under specific exceptions.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §159

A4.t:
**Answer.** Confessions made to a police officer cannot be used as evidence against the person who made them, unless the confession is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate.

**Why.** The law generally prohibits the use of any confession made by a person while they are in the custody of a police officer, unless that confession is made in the immediate presence of a Magistrate. This rule applies regardless of the nature of the offense.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §23

items.q: What is the implication for the party's reliance on the evidence of its own witness?
items.ref: The party remains entitled to rely on any part of the witness's evidence, despite being allowed to ask it questions.

A1.t:
**Answer.** A party's reliance on the evidence of its own witness implies that the party has placed significant trust in the veracity of that witness's testimony.

**Why.** When a party relies on the evidence of its own witness, it indicates an expectation that the witness will provide truthful and accurate testimony, which can influence the credibility assessment by the court.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** The party that calls a witness can rely on any part of the evidence given by that witness, even if the witness is later questioned about matters outside the scope of the original examination.

**Why.** This rule allows the party that has called a witness to benefit fully from the testimony provided, regardless of any subsequent questioning that may challenge the original statements or introduce new information.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §157

A3.t:
**Answer.** The party cannot rely on the evidence of any witness who has been called by it.

**Why.** The law stipulates that no party shall be allowed to rely upon the evidence of any witness who has been called by that party.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §348

A4.t:
**Answer.** The party that calls the witness retains the right to rely on any part of the evidence given by that witness, even if the Court permits the adverse party to ask questions during cross-examination.

**Why.** The law provides that the Court may permit the person who calls a witness to put any question to him which might be put in cross-examination by the adverse party. Crucially, this permission does not affect the party's right to rely on any part of the evidence given by that witness.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §157

items.q: What is the implication of using words in describing an offence in a charge?
items.ref: The words used will be interpreted in the sense attached to them by the law under which the offence is punishable.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The use of specific words in describing an offence in a charge is crucial as it must accurately reflect the nature of the alleged crime to ensure the accused understands the charges against them.

**Why.** Precise wording is essential to ensure that the accused is aware of the exact nature of the charges and can prepare a proper defense. The description must conform to the provisions of the relevant statute to avoid any ambiguity or misinterpretation.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** The words used in describing an offence in a charge shall be deemed to have the meaning given to them by the law under which the offence is punishable.

**Why.** This ensures clarity and consistency in the description of the offence, aligning the terminology used in the charge with the legal definitions provided by the relevant statute to avoid any ambiguity.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §237

A3.t:
**Answer.** The use of words in describing an offence in a charge is deemed to be an essential part of that charge.

**Why.** The law stipulates that when words are used to describe an offence in a charge, these words are considered an integral and essential component of that charge.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §219

A4.t:
**Answer.** Words used in describing an offence in a charge are deemed to have been used in the sense attached to them by the law under which the offence is punishable.

**Why.** The law dictates that when words are used in describing an offence in a charge, those words are deemed to have been used in the sense attached to them by the law under which the offence is punishable.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §237

items.q: What is the implication when an offence is committed by a member of an unlawful assembly in prosecution of the common object?
items.ref: Every person who was a member of the same assembly at the time of the committing of the offence is considered guilty of that offence.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The members of an unlawful assembly can be prosecuted individually for the common object even if not all members were present at the scene of the crime.

**Why.** This provision ensures that all members of an unlawful assembly who share the common object are held accountable, regardless of their physical presence during the commission of the offense.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §54

A2.t:
**Answer.** Every person who, at the time of the committing of that offence, is a member of the same assembly, is guilty of that offence.

**Why.** This rule holds all members of an unlawful assembly criminally responsible for the offences committed by any member in pursuit of the common object of the assembly, based on the principle of collective responsibility.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §190

A3.t:
**Answer.** The law presumes that every member of the assembly was present and participated in the commission of the offence.

**Why.** When an offence is committed by a member of an unlawful assembly while prosecuting the common object, the law makes a presumption that every member of the assembly was present and took part in the commission of the offence.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, §194

A4.t:
**Answer.** Every person who, at the time of the committing of that offence, is a member of the same assembly, is guilty of that offence.

**Why.** If an offence is committed by any member of an unlawful assembly in prosecution of the common object of that assembly, or such as the members of that assembly knew to be likely to be committed in prosecution of that object, every person who, at the time of the committing of that offence, is a member of the same assembly, is guilty of that offence.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, §190

items.q: What is the implication when one party in a contract fails to provide something that is necessary for the other party to perform their promise?
items.ref: The non-performing party is bound to make compensation to the other party for any loss caused by the non-performance.

A1.t:
**Answer.** The contract is voidable at the option of the other party.

**Why.** When a party to a contract fails to provide something essential for the performance of the contract, the other party has the right to treat the contract as voidable and may seek remedies such as rescission or damages.

**Source.** The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, §24

A2.t:
**Answer.** The contract becomes voidable at the option of the party whose performance is dependent on the other party's promise. This party can choose to terminate the contract and seek compensation for any loss sustained due to the non-performance.

**Why.** When one party's obligation is contingent on the other party fulfilling their promise, the failure of the latter to do so means the former cannot be compelled to fulfill their part of the agreement. Therefore, the contract can be terminated by the affected party, who can also claim compensation for any losses incurred as a result of the non-performance.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §53

A3.t:
**Answer.** The failure of one party to furnish what is necessary for the other party to perform their promise discharges the latter from their obligation.

**Why.** If one party fails to furnish what is necessary for the other party to perform his promise, the latter is discharged from his obligation.

**Source.** The Indian Contract Act, 1872, §50

A4.t:
